STAR WARS TRILOGY EVERYTHING OLD IS NEW AGAIN article by Mark Cotta Vaz In the beginning, Star Wars was derided as creator George Lucas' impossible dream. But the film's 1977 release - which transported global movie audiences into the midst of a civil war set 'a long time ago in a galaxy far, far away' - ultimately generated record-breaking boxoffice revenues, as well as the sequels The Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi. With the 1983 release of the last film, the trilogy had presented core chapters four through six of a sweeping, nine-part saga envisioned by Lucas, But while the growing Lucasfilm entertainment empire continued to stoke the fires of Star Wars mythology in best-selling novels, comic books, interactive games and other media, calendar years peeled off without a flicker of new big-screen adventures. One reason for the lack of new Star Wars feature installments was that - at the time of Return of the Jedi's release - Lucas and his famed Industrial Light & Magic effects unit had come close to hitting the wall in terms of otherworldly visions that could be created with physical materials and photochemically-based optical printing. But ILM's subsequent pioneering into the digital realm - explorations that culminated in the breakthrough computer graphics dinosaurs of Jurassic Park - not only paved the way for a Star Wars 'prequel' trilogy that would comprise chapters one through three of the epic, but a return to the original trilogy itself. The latter 'Special Edition' project would see ILM entering into the alchemical secrets of the classic trilogy, a bit of time traveling that would fuse the verities of the original movies with the modern magic of a digital era. Lucasfilm's plan was to celebrate the twentieth anniversary of the seminal Star Wars installment - since christened A New Hope - with a theatrical Twenty years after launching the phenomenally successfulStar Wars series, creator George Lucas has revamped some of the effects he long found lacking - and added a few new scenes - for a 'Special Edition' theatrical reissue of the trilogy. release of an enhanced version of the classic. ILM digital tools would be employed to repair tell-tale optical effects, integrate computer generated creatures and cityscapes within existing footage, provide new cuts to both expand on and replicate sequences, and generally bring the film up to date for modern audiences accustomed to nearly flawless visual effects spectacle. The trick would be to retain the original film in all the digital tinkering. No new characters and plot lines would be introduced; and ILM's digital spruce-up would have to reproduce the lower-tech aesthetic of that earlier filmmaking and effects era. For George Lucas, the Special Edition was an opportunity to enrich and restore A New Hope to what he had seen in his mind's eye all along - but which, because of the limitations of time and technology, had not entirely made it to film. "I think George was a little embarrassed by the success of Star Wars," said Lucasfilm producer Rick McCallum. "Despite the adulation, he'd made so many compromises during production that his dream had not been fulfilled. But since George foresaw the direction that filmmaking and digital technology were going with such clarity, he resolved that, given the chance, he would fulfill his original dream. Now, nearly twenty years later, he is able to say: 'At the beginning, I didn't have the resources, the technology, or the support - but now I have those things.' To me, that is such an innocent and romantic notion - to go back and make the film in exactly the way he envisioned it, no more or less." The fulfillment of that dream would take two and a half years - the same length of time it took to make the original movie. By the early months of 1996, the Special Edition assignment had been expanded to include both The Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi; and plans had been made to release the Star Wars Trilogy Special Edition in a staggered 1997 schedule. In addition to righting Lucas' thwarted dreams for the original movies, the Special Edition project would serve as a launching pad and research and development lab for the long-awaited Star Wars prequels, slated to begin CINEFEX 69 • 15

Footage of Harrison Ford as Solo had actually been shot for the original film, but the scene had never been realized because of the failure to produce an acceptable Jabba creature effect. While Lucas' personal reconstruction plans centered on the Mos Eisley sequence, others at ILM - notably, veterans of the original Star Wars productions - wanted their own second crack at the classic films. "I laid out about a dozen to two dozen shots I'd always wanted to redo," remarked Dennis Muren, a second cameraman on A New Hope who spearheaded the Special Edition conceptual stage and provided consulting help throughout the long effort. Whereas the original Jedi had ended with Luke and company celebrating the demise of the evil Empire with Ewoks on Endor's forest moon, the Special Edition would add shots to reveal galaxywide rejoicing, with a never-before-seen big-screen glimpse of the Imperial city of Coruscant. While Lucas initiated the project and retained final approval on all redos and additional scenes, Rick McCallum headed the Trilogy Special Edition production effort, coordinating ILM's assignment with visual effects producer Tom Kennedy, and with Dave Carson, who would supervise the visual effects on the Empire and Jedi editions. The New Hope refurbishment kicked off with Dennis Muren and the production art department developing concept sketches that included gigantic, lizardlike dewbacks, rat-like scurriers to scuttle through the dusty streets of an enhanced Mos Eisley, and expansive new views of that spaceport city. It was during this early phase that Lucas and other Special Edition principals, while reviewing New Hope prints for possible redo work, noticed the film's alarming pits and scratches and faded color. A warning flag went up at both Lucasfilm's offices and at Twentieth Century Fox, the studio that had released the trilogy. It was soon discovered that, although the film had been properly stored in the studio's Midwest subterranean vaults, the original negative had an overall ten to fifteen percent loss of once vibrant color, and the negative itself was crusted with dirt. Thus, the New Hope Special Edition project grew to include the restoration of the original negative - a team effort headed up by Lucasfilm and Twentieth Century Fox and augmented by Pacific Title, where state-of-the-art optical printers were employed to recomposite the original elements for wipes, skip-frames and other shots identified as 'bread-and-butter' opticals. YCM Labs was charged with color timing corrections, and film restorer Leon Briggs was retained for overall guidance and consultation services. Lucas' foresight in saving the original optical elements aided the restoration effort tremendously. In addition, a special Technicolor Star Wars print in Lucas' possession - which utilized the 'threestrip' process first introduced in 1932 - provided YCM's color-timing crew with a record of the film's original color. Once restored, the specific footage designated for Special Edition enhancement could then be sent on to ILM. Although Empire and Jedi would likewise require some restoration work, the sequels had not suffered New Hope's level of damage - a credit to their higher production values and bigger budgets. In contrast, the trailblazing New Hope had been a patchwork production cut through with four different film stocks, including a Kodak color stock that was subsequently found to be prone to fading and was discontinued shortly after the picture's release. The services of outside optical houses had also been needed in order for ILM to meet its deadline, adding to the patchwork quality. By the time Empire went into production, ILM had relocated from Southern California to Marin County, where it was organized and restructured in such a way that Lucas' effects division could consolidate its operation and handle all its opticals in-house. "By that time," said Tom Kennedy, "ILM was up and running CINEFEX 69 • 17

To accommodate the new digital elements, ILM match-movers Sel Eddy and Terry Chostner needed to duplicate the original camera moves with their virtual camera - taking into account the minute adjustments and unique vibrations of twenty-year-old cameras. The film grain normally added to CG elements also had to duplicate the exact consistency of grain in the original scene. "We had to stay consistent throughout the trilogy and not try to 'wow' the audience with something obviously new," Kennedy related. "A new Special Edition element had to look like an extension of the original intent - so if someone other than an aficionado were to look at the film for the first time, an enhanced scene wouldn't stand out as a different type of scene." This marriage of old and new presented the thorniest challenges for the digital compositors. Particularly vexing for senior compositor Tom Rosseter - who had joined ILM's optical department for Empire and later segued into digital - was the recompositing of Jedi shots of Jabba's sail barge flying over sand dunes surrounding the Sarlacc Pit. "We had problems with the resolution and the blur, because when the barge started moving quickly there was a lot of blue spill," said Rosseter. "Back then, the bluescreen was basically shot with Nikon lenses - the kind you'd buy for your still camera. They were very good lenses for their time, but they were never meant to handle the amount of blue we get from a bluescreen. We got away with some of those shots back then, but only because of the way George used them - how fast he'd cut, or the way he'd draw the eye to a particular point in the frame so the problem areas wouldn't be noticeable." One of the greatest recompositing challenges was the snowspeeder-versus-Imperial-walker scene in Empire, a daylight battle staged on the icy fields of planet Hoth. Nearly one hundred original snow battle shots - gray-over-white composites - had to be recomposited within a very short time. During the film's late-seventies production period, ILM's optical department had labored mightily on the battle. "We knew the Hoth sequence was going to be difficult, even then," recalled Bruce Nicholson. "The background plates had been shot in Norway, and there was a lot of overcast - so, against that opaque background, the composited speeder element looked very cut-out. We employed a variety of techniques to deal with those problems, such as doing flash exposures on the speeders to blend them into the snowy background. Techniques like that helped; but, nonetheless, in terms of the matte work, there certainly were flaws. All of those shots have been improved, thanks to the control digital techniques have given us over matte edges." The Hoth battle sequence also suffered from transparency problems, such as insufficiently dense snow field background mattes seeping into foreground bluescreen elements of Luke Skywalker's snowspeeder cockpit. The transparencies were cleaned up by Dave Carson and his team in the digital recompositing process. ILM's tool of choice for quick recomposites was the in-house Sabre, a digital compositing and editing system, based on Discreet Logic's Flame, that had been developed for The Young Indiana Jones Chronicles. Perhaps the best example of ILM's digital renovation of existing footage was for the sequence in New Hope in which Han Solo, sauntering into a Mos Eisley hangar to check on his Millennium Falcon, discovers Jabba the Hutt and some underworld hirelings awaiting him. The incident was to initiate a thread that would run through the entire trilogy, with Hutt's anger at a double-cross culminating in Solo's imprisonment in a slab of carbonite at the climax of Empire, and his later being displayed in Jabba's palace in Jedi. The confrontation in the first movie had been filmed with Harrison Ford on a hangar set, with a nondescript actor playing the Jabba role. The footage was cut from the film, however, when the actor's performance was deemed inappropriate for the embodiment of the galactic underworld, and the limited effects technology of the day could not produce a more convincing character. The result was that the specter of Jabba was left to float behind the scenes until Return of the Jedi when he was produced as a gigantic animatronic effect. Armed with its new digital tools, however, ILM could create a much more dynamic Jabba for the Special Edition, and return the character's seminal scene to its rightful place in A New Hope. Animated by Steve Williams, the computer generated Jabba moves in undulating, slug-like fashion through the hangar, even interacting with Ford as the actor seemingly steps on the crime lord's tail. For good measure, Boba Fett - the bounty hunter who would appear in Empire - was added into the scene as a bluescreen element of an actor costumed in the original Fett outfit. The actor portraying Jabba in the original footage had to be painstakingly replaced in the digital revision, with areas of the plate in which the CG creation did not fully cover the human performer also recreated digitally. To sell the interaction of the two characters - separated in execution by twenty years - Harrison Ford's eyeline had to sync up precisely with Jabba's positioning. As a result, Williams had to work backwards, animating his character to coincide with Ford's eyelines, rather than letting the animation lead the scene. "We could not just digitally reanimate Harrison Ford's eyeline," Kennedy explained, "because eyelines are determined not just by the position of the eyeball, but by body posture as well. Other challenges involved integrating the new Jabba with the older film's grain structure and exposure variations, and dealing with various filters. Some of the original scenes had been filmed with a net in front of the camera, much like a nylon or silk stocking, and we had to match the characteristics of its effect on the images, particularly in highlight areas." The new Cloud City sequence included three arrival shots - a cockpit view, a fly-though shot of the ship maneuvering through canyons of cyindrical skyscrapers, and a final landing approach - all of which had to match the original scene's set architecture and twilight-hour lighting. Art director George Hull first established the look and pacing of the new shots using storyboards and wire-frame animatics. Many new Cloud City buildings were then constructed with ILM's own interactive Viewpaint texture mapping software, which allowed digital artists to paint hundreds of textures directly onto 3-D wire-frame surfaces. "The amount of detail in a photograph of a city is staggering," Carson stated, "so there was a limit to how much visual information we could put into Cloud City. There were also continuity concerns, since the Cloud City we had to cut with wasn't heavily detailed. It had a sparse, but elegant feel. We struggled with maintaining that sparse style while still coming up with enough visual detail to make the buildings look real." The Empire Special Edition would also feature a glorious Cloud City morning scene of Princess Leia gazing from the window of a building - redone as a computer generated structure so that ILM's digital artists could create a more pleasing composition by centering Leia in the picture window. In contrast to the relatively forgiving twilight illumination in the fly-through shots, the morning scene presented the problem of rendering CG buildings and passing orange cloud cars in bright, revealing sunlight. "The huge amount of visual information we have to provide when something is in bright sunlight is really a strain," Carson explained, "and the computer doesn't do it automatically. Someone has to make all the choices regarding the lighting, how rough the surface materials are and how they treat light, the color of the light, the bounce light - all the things that determine the final rendered image. It is a very time-consuming, trial-and-error process, with no magical measuring device to let us know how far off we are from reality. We have to look at renders on the monitor, filming them out as we get closer to a final. Judging those shots on film is another step, in which we determine how the image is going to be modified as it goes from the digital to the film world." Since most of the original Cloud City scenes had been played out in interior rooms and generic corridors, Lucas asked that the Special Edition work include glimpses of the entrancing exterior. One such shot - which began as a simple imageprocessing makeover to clean up flickering in the plate and other minor flaws - featured Princess Leia running down an interior hallway with Chewbacca. "George said, Let's pull the characters out and put a new background in there," commented Tom Rosseter. "He wanted to see an exterior view that would reveal that night was falling. So Julia Adrianson took the same characters running in the foreground, but placed them in a painted sunset environment. Since the characters were now illuminated by a sunset rather than interior lighting, all of the colors and reflections had to be changed. It improved the shot a lot because it suggested where the characters were heading better than the original." The town of Mos Eisley also underwent a facelift - courtesy of Yusei Uesugi and Paul Huston of the digital matte department - and, in its reincarnation, became the bustling city Lucas had always visualized. Huston's slate of new Mos Eisley shots included a scene in which a landspeeder bearing Luke, the droids and Obi-Wan makes its entrance into the city. The shot featured a camera point-ofview ten feet above the vehicle as it coasted down a narrow street flanked by stucco-like buildings, as well as Mos Eisley pedestrians, a hulking droid and scurriers. While the environment would consist of Huston's digital matte paintings, and the pedestrians were bluescreened extras in costume, the droid, scurriers and even the landspeeder and its occupants were all computer generated. Scanned images of physical miniatures shot in natural sunlight provided the foundation for the Mos Eisley environment, and were combined - through the cut-and-paste capabilities of Photoshop - with other digital images. "Rough building textures and outdoor lighting are still hard to do in CG, but easy to do in miniatures," Huston stated. "When first looking at this shot, I realized that I could make some fairly crude models with simple texturing materials, paint them, then put them outside and photograph them. I shot them at the correct camera height to get the proper perspective: then, once in digital, I could fix edges and colors, take out things that didn't look right and add subtle details such as a crack along a wall. It was a lot easier than starting out in the computer and having to add all the subtleties that make something look real." The miniature was five feet wide and twenty feet deep, and consisted of a dusty road flanked by two rows of buildings. Sculpting the buildings out of foam board covered with spackling compound, Huston added a funky effects flourish for the distant background by placing painted trash cans in forced perspective. After photographing the models outdoors, Huston supervised the live-action bluescreen shoot - also conducted outside so that the lighting could be duplicated. "The lighting on the miniatures determined at what time and angle we would have to shoot the bluescreen plates," stated Huston. "To perfectly emulate the lighting on the model, we had about a two-hour window of opportunity to film the live-action." The shot of Luke's landspeeder entering Mos Eisley was one of the breakthrough images of the entire Special Edition project - a panoramic view that pushed the limits of digital matte painting techniques. The camera starts out on the cruising landspeeder, then booms up to the rooftops of the mosque-like city structures, revealing not only pedestrians below but distant mountains and a half-dozen spacecraft in the blue sky above. Once again, bluescreen pedestrians and CG elements of the landspeeder and flying spaceships were integrated into a fabricated environment; but, whereas Huston combined physical model photography with digital paint techniques for his Mos Eisley images, the establishing view - executed by Yusei Uesugi - was created with digital paint alone. The complexity of the shot grew as Lucas asked for an ever-expanding camera move. To avoid the burdensome rendering effort that would be needed to realize the wide-scoped shot through conventional digital techniques, Uesugi brainstormed a breakthrough projection effect. "George requested more and more camera moves," Uesugi recalled, "until I realized I couldn't do it with just a single painting. So I came up with the idea of setting up perspective points and selectively compositing painted textures." After first incorporating all the lighting, shadow and surface details directly onto his digital painting, Uesugi projected the image onto a rough 3-D cityscape model constructed of wire-frame and a plain modeled surface. Unlike a CG model created in three-dimensional space, the projection approach provided the illusion of perspective and dimensionality without intensive processing time. TURBULENCE TERROR IN THE SKIES article by Ted Elrick In the Rysher Entertainment thriller Turbulence, a quiet, nearly empty Christmas Eve flight between New York and Los Angeles becomes a nightmare for flight attendant Teri Halloran (Lauren Holly) when convicted serial killer Ryan Weaver (Ray Liotta) and armed robber Stubbs (Brendan Gleeson) board her jetliner in the custody of federal marshals. During a bloody escape attempt, the marshals and Stubbs are eliminated, along with most of the flight crew, leaving only Halloran in command. To save herself and the passengers, she must maneuver the jumbo jet through the heart of a Level 6 storm and land it safely in Los Angeles - all the while engaging in a high-stakes game of cat and mouse with the psychotic Weaver. Director Robert Butler - a veteran of hit television shows such as Hill Street Blues, Moonlighting and Lois & Clark - would rely on visual effects supervisor and second unit director Mark Vargo, Boss Film Studios and the support of Pacific Title Digital to provide the crucial storm footage. A former Boss staff member, Vargo had recently segued into projects that were production oriented, rather than effects intensive. But when offered the assignment for Turbulence, Vargo could not resist the challenge. Part of the project's appeal was that it would require Vargo - along with director of aerial photography David Nowell - to spend a full week airborne, storm-chasing throughout the Pacific Northwest to record aerial footage of the Boeing 747 leased by the production. That footage would be combined and intercut with model photography, and enhanced with digital storm effects. "I enjoy pulling shots off and making them look real," said Vargo. "I didn't think there'd ever been a movie in which the flying stuff - cross-cutting footage of a model with footage of a real airplane in flight - In Turbulence - a Robert Butler film with visual effects by Boss Film Studios and Pacific Title Digital - a young flight attendant must pilot a 747 jetliner across country, through a major storm, while fending off a psychotic killer. looked totally convincing." As dictated by the Jonathan Brett screenplay, Turbulence begins with the plane's takeoff just before sunset, and continues into night, Air-to-air daylight exteriors and some day-for-night footage of the 747 encountering air turbulence were shot by Vargo and Nowell from a Lear jet using a snorkel lens camera system. "There isn't a Lear jet built that has a clear plexiglass window for shooting out the side," Vargo commented, "so the snorkel system is essential for side shots - even though it limits the exposures you can use." To capture actual night footage for climactic shots of the plane approaching Los Angeles, a vintage B-25 bomber, equipped with a full-size motion picture camera for shooting in less available light, was employed in place of the Lear. "In a Lear jet, a full-size camera can only be mounted in the nose," Vargo stated. "It's a fixed mount with the camera locked off in one position - so the pilot essentially dictates the shot by how he approaches the plane being photographed. I wanted to have more control and be able to shoot from a variety of angles. The B-25 - with its huge glass bubble on the front - not only gave us room to vary our camera angles, it also allowed us to change lenses and film magazines while airborne. With a full-size camera in the Lear, we would have had to land and reload. A drawback of the B-25, however, was that it couldn't fly fast enough to keep up with the 747 at cruising speed - which is why we also had the Lear. Using both airplanes, we were able to get all of the liveaction footage we needed for the entire crosscountry flight." Shots of the plane in the Level 6 storm could not be captured during the live-action shoot, due to the inherent dangers of piloting a jet through a storm of that magnitude. The solution was to digitally enhance the live-action footage to create dramatic images of the plane within the tempest. 101 DALMATIANS PUPPY PROLIFERATION article by Jody Duncan In 1961, Walt Disney Pictures continued its 24-year winning streak in producing successful full-length animated movies with 101 Dalmatians, a boy-meets-girl, boy-dog-meets-girl-dog story, told from the canines' point of view. Based on a popular children's book by Dodie Smith, 101 Dalmatians featured talking animals with defined personalities, and enough Dalmatian puppies to populate firehouses around the world - fanciful elements that made cel animation the ideal medium for the full-length film. Thirty-five years later - armed with 3-D animation tools and improved animatronics technology - the Disney studio, director Stephen Herek and producer/writer John Hughes succeeded in making a vivid live-action version of the animated classic. Launching the holiday movie season with its November 1996 release, 101 Dalmatians had much of the wholesome appeal of the original, plus a topnotch cast that included Glenn Close as fur-crazy villainess Cruella De Vil and Jeff Daniels and Joely Richardson as Dalmatian 'pets' Roger and Anita. Non-human roles such as Dalmatians Pongo and Perdita, their rambunctious litter of puppies, a commanding Airedale named Kipper and various raccoons, cows, pigs and sheep were as crucial to the film as the two-legged characters; and months before cameras rolled at Shepperton Studios, near London, a three-pronged strategy for realizing those animal performances was carefully devised. Going for a realistic style, Herek sought to get as many of his shots as possible with real dogs and other animals, relying on animal consultant Gary Gero and his team of trainers to wrangle filmworthy performances from the creatures. Shots that could not be captured live would be turned over to visual In 101 Dalmatians, actor Jeff Daniels strokes a newborn puppy - one of fifty puppet dogs created by the Jim Henson Creature Shop to augment the live animals used predominantly in the show. / Henson effects supervisor Neal Scanlan fits a head skin onto one of the animatronic creations. effects supervisor Michael Owens - who, with a team from Industrial Light & Magic, would create photorealistic, 3-D animated canine characters - or to creature effects supervisor Neal Scanlan and the Jim Henson Creature Shop, responsible for building animatronic stand-in critters. The digital effects portion of the plan was so important that ILM was brought onto the show a full five months before the start of production. The company's earliest efforts were dedicated to providing storyboards for the 3-D animation scenes. "That early on," noted Michael Owens, "they didn't really know what they wanted in the way of visual effects. They had questions as to what the capabilities of 3-D animation were, what the current state of the art was. We told them that the approaching state of the art was replication - real and computer animated characters together in the same shot. We were confident that we could pull that off." Owens' confidence was firm, despite the fact that neither ILM nor any other effects facility had ever accomplished such a feat. "In its own way," remarked animation supervisor Tom Bertino, "101 Dalmatians was as much a groundbreaker as anything we've done before. Putting a CG Dalmatian puppy into a live-action plate with real Dalmatian pups may not seem to be as big a deal as creating a T-rex for Jurassic Park - it wouldn't have the audience going 'ooh' and 'ahh' in quite the same way - but in terms of the work we do here, it was at least as important, if not more so. We were attempting to create something that people are very familiar with, and put it right next to the real thing where it would be in direct comparison. Slipping CG characters into live-action shots, undetected, and mixing them with the real dogs was a gutsy thing to do." Before committing to that gutsy act, Owens and team conducted a test, shooting real puppies on stage at ILM, then applying digital manipulation techniques to the footage. "We did splits and some 2-D manipulation of the real puppy elements," said Owens. "We also replicated one dog - although CINEFEX 69 • 41

we didn't take it to a final stage. It was just meant to illustrate what was possible." With production a few months away, and the script still being developed, the scope and exact nature of ILM's work remained nebulous, even after the test was approved. One of the key issues to be resolved was the degree of personality with which to endow the film's central characters - Pongo and Perdy's fifteen Dalmatian puppies. "In the original animated movie," commented Owens, "some of the puppies were literally characters with distinct personalities. We told them we could do that, if they chose to go that way." Two-dimensional manipulation of the real puppy footage was one way in which 42 * CINEFEX 69 touches of personality could be added, a technique Owens had demonstrated in his test. "Through something like Elastic Reality, we could do a shift of a puppy eyebrow, for example, which was simple and looked great in the test. But, ultimately, they chose to play down personality traits in the dogs and present them very realistically." Associate visual effects supervisor Doug Smythe oversaw the development and modification of software in preparation for the 3-D assignment. With the technology in place, Owens looked for inspiration in nature, bringing in real Dalmatian puppies to the facility, and filming them for reference. "For a while that summer," recalled Owens, "we were imIndustrial Light & Magic contributed a number of elaborate split-screen composites, as well as digital matte paintings and wire removals. porting puppies on a regular basis. We would put them on the floor and shoot them with three cameras, or use a Steadicam to follow them around. From that we accumulated a library of study footage. We also continued to bring puppies in on a biweekly basis so that the modelers and animators could see and study the real thing." "That was the best part of our research period," Bertino added. "Playing with puppies - yeah, that was hard to take. We had our whole crew in on it, plus a lot of gate-crashers who just couldn't resist coming in to play with a floor full of puppies." To give them a starting point in building a CG model, Owens and his digital team attempted to scan a real puppy - as they would a maquette - but quickly learned the severe limitations of puppy attention span. Motion capture techniques were also tested as a means to achieve gross body movements - which would have left animators free to concentrate on more subtle performance animation - but that approach was also abandoned. "We found that it is pretty difficult to put little sensors on puppies and have them stay on," said Bertino. "They chewed them off immediately." The other problem with using motion capture for the project was that, at the time, the technology had not yet fully matured. "Motion capture wasn't quite there," noted Owens. "The bugs were just getting worked out, and it wasn't a great production tool yet - we were just a couple of months too early. Even now, motion capture isn't an end-all answer to everything; but I think it would have helped ease some of the problems. We could have had the trainers put the puppies through actions - which would have been motion captured - and then we could have plugged those movements into the computer model. I think the result could have been wonderful. We did a test, and it was promising; but motion capture just wasn't production oriented yet. Also, since we did not know what the volume of shots would end up being, we had to go a more sure route; and with the relatively small number of shots we had, it was probably just as well that we animated them through the usual techniques." Those usual techniques included the building and scanning of a physical maquette. "It was just an initial step to help us understand the proportions of a puppy," Owens explained. THE SIXTH MAN HOOP SCHEMES article by Estelle Shay Evidenced by such enduring motion pictures as The Ghost and Mrs. Muir and A Guy Named Joe, or the more recent, but no less memorable, Heart and Souls and Ghost, the spirit realm has long held a particular fascination for Hollywood filmmakers. Though techniques as simple as mirror gags and double exposures have been used to produce ghostly images, today such projects are more likely to utilize sophisticated digital effects to breathe life into their spectral incarnations. A case in point is Touchstone Pictures' upcoming comedy, The Sixth Man, directed by Randall Miller, in which a young basketball star, unexpectedly struck down in his prime, returns in ghostly form to create bedlam on the playing courts. The screenplay, by Christopher Reed and C.N. Carle, centers on the relationship between two brothers - Kenny (Marlon Wayans) and Antoine Tyler (Kadeem Hardison) - whose dreams of making it to the NCAA basketball finals are cut short when Antoine suffers a fatal heart attack during a game. Demoralized by the loss of their superstar player, Antoine's teammates plunge into a losing streak until Kenny's frustrated cry for help unwittingly summons forth his brother's supercharged ghost - unpredictable, mischievous and hellbent on leading his team to victory at any cost. With Antoine's ghostly antics figuring prominently in the story, Miller turned for visual effects support to John Van Vliet, whose company, Available Light, had been responsible for a number of cutting-edge visual effects in the hit film Ghost six years earlier. "The script was kind of fun," stated Van Vliet. "But another reason we were attracted to the project was that so much has changed since Ghost, which was sort of the last big blockbuster effects movie that wasn't all digital. And although that show did phenomenally well on the strength In The Sixth Man - a Randall Miller comedy with visual effects by Available Light - a young basketball star, stricken with a fatal heart attack. returns as a ghost to help his teammates. of good talent and good directing, working on it was really frustrating because the optical process was slow and rather limiting. The prospect of going back and doing similar shots with today's tools was really exciting." During two months of preproduction, starting in March 1996, Available Light began planning its approach to the modestly budgeted film with an eye towards efficiency and economy. "In addition to cable and wire removal,"stated Van Vliet, "there were a number of shots involving pass-throughs or body possessions as the ghost of Antoine jumps in and out of people and performs other assorted high-jinx to make his presence felt. So we began by figuring as many different ways as we could to do these kinds of effects." While simple means were used whenever possible, Van Vliet would ultimately rely heavily on 2-D and 3-D computer generated imagery for many of the shots. "That was a first for us. Normally we have more of a blend of optical and digital. But with digital technology, we found that the level of fidelity in a simple thing like a pass-through was quantum leaps ahead of the effects in Ghost. I'm always the first to admit I really distrust and dislike computers - I truly think they're tools of the devil - but I will happily use any tool I can get my hands on if it's going to make a cool movie. In order to oversee the heavy digital workload, Van Vliet elected to remain at his Burbank facility during most of the forty-day shoot, filmed at major basketball venues in Washington and Vancouver, British Columbia. Recruited to supervise on-set plate and greenscreen photography was frequent Available Light collaborator Steve Moore. As the movie opens, Antoine is stricken with a heart attack during a game while performing his trademark slam dunk. Letting go his grasp on the rim of the basket, he plunges to the floor as his teammates rush to his aid. To film the fall, Moore shot the actor dropping into a greenscreen airbag, which would later be replaced with the hardwood CINEFEX 69 • 49

floor. "To make the fall more dramatic," said Van Vliet, "we did a little twist on reality by pulling the whole net assembly up to about fifteen feet - much higher than it would normally be - and shooting with a wide lens, with the camera overcranked." Though the sequence was initially conceived with the idea that the shot would cut away at the moment of impact, the director subsequently decided to have the camera linger on the stricken player. "Since the airbag folded around Kadeem's body as he fell into it, we had to go in and reconstruct all the edges - which entailed huge amounts of work." A separate plate was used to split in footage of the teammates rushing in. Unwittingly summoned back by his younger brother, the ghost of Antoine materializes before Kenny's eyes in the locker room following a game. In distraught disbelief, Kenny takes a swing at the ghost, attempting to dispel the presumed hallucination. As the ineffectual punch passes through Antoine's head, it wildly distorts his ectoplasmic face. "That effect wasn't planned," recalled Van Vliet. "We were literally on the set when the director suggested it. So we collected footage of Marlon Wayans swinging his closed fist through the air that would allow us to do a simple pass-through. 50 1 CINEFEX 69 Before investing in a lot of computer time, however, we did a 'slop comp' - a quick optical, just like in the old days - to see how it would play." Having determined that the interaction was too quick and the effect virtually invisible, Van Vliet suggested throwing in a slight distortion to extend it. "Randy took that idea and ran with it, proposing something far more exaggerated, like in The Mask. In line with that, we had one of our animators, Carl Fornander, traditionally hand-animate a face stretch. Once a satisfactory version was achieved, we scanned the test into the computer and used the pencil animation as a guide for 2-D animation and paint techniques. Cynthia Hyland accomplished much of it using Photoshop and Elastic Reality on a Macintosh platform." For the following shot - a view from behind in which a bulge in the shape of Kenny's fist emerges through the back of Antoine's head - digital artist Scott Coulter built a 3-D computer generated fist using Lightwave, and covered it with a stretchy surface. Zany things begin to happen on the basketball court as Antoine, invisible to his teammates, begins interfering with their game in an effort to help them win. While many of the stunts were done as wire gags, rigged by Thomas Special Effects under For a scene of the ghost being punched, Available Light used hand-drawn animation as a guide for a digitally rendered cartoony effect. the direction of Stewart Bradley, other sequences - particularly those in which Antoine inhabits the bodies of unsuspecting players - required digital intervention. "Because budget was such a huge consideration on this show, we had planned originally on having locked backgrounds for many of those shots so that we could do split-screens; but when it came time to shoot the plates, we found ourselves dealing with wild backgrounds - which were not real effects friendly. So nearly all of the shots required a lot of roto work." Digital artists Cynthia Hyland and Warren Fuller experimented with the possession plates, attempting to embellish the standard pass-through effects called for in the original storyboards. "We built a Chinese menu," Van Vliet elaborated. "We would do a shot four or five times, trying option A or option B, faster or slower, so the director could pick pieces and arrange them." A watery effect - dubbed 'glass man' by the digital team - was developed to signal ghostly transitions. "It was our own witch's brew of filters. Nothing hideously complex - just a displacement process that reacted to highlights and contrast. Mixed and matched in just the right ratio, it was sort of like three-dimensional ripple glass. We also did things such as soften the edges of the ghost and give him a weird motion streak. Then we would inflate the clothes of the character who was being possessed, so that it looked like there was a change of mass, and alter his color slightly." A number of on-court scenes had the basketball flying through the air in a variety of radical, wacky moves orchestrated by Antoine. A computer generated basketball was used in place of the real ball for those shots. However, an episode in which the ball appears to come to life in the hands of an opposing team player was done principally as a practical effect. In the sequence, a closeup shot of the ball reveals its surface morphing into the features of Antoine and snarling a warning to the startled player. "We could have done it all in 3-D," stated Van Vliet, "but to get the kind of nuanced facial expressions we wanted, the cost would have been equivalent to the defense budget of Morocco - and we'd probably still be working on it." Instead, Van Vliet opted to accomplish the sequence using the real actor's face in combination with several fiberglass models built by Todd Masters (continued on page 55) HUSKIES

DANTE'S INFERNO article by Rita Street

Although the Pacific Northwest region is dotted with volcanic peaks, inhabitants had co-existed with these sleeping giants for millennia, without incident. In fact, there had been no cataclysmic volcanic eruption on North American soil since Mount Mazama, in a blast of titanic proportions, formed six-mile-wide Crater Lake some seven thousand years ago. So when, in early 1980, a series of small earthquakes began to rumble through a mountainous region of southwestern Washington, few residents recognized their significance. The local myopia did not stop Mount St. Helens from fulfilling her destiny, however: and on May 18, the long-dormant volcano erupted with a suddenness and severity that took not only the state of Washington, but the entire world, by surprise. For those who observed from a safe distance, news broadcasts and surreal photographs of the angry, spewing mountain and its aftermath - images of indomitable force and total devastation - engendered awe and a kind of morbid fascination. In a massive landslide caused by the eruption of gases and lava through the cone, nearly half of Mount St. Helens slid fifteen miles into the valley below. What followed immediately thereafter was even more catastrophic: a superheated mixture of gas and ash - called a pyroclastic flow-spewed out of the earth, forming a several-mile-wide cloud that resembled nothing so much as a nuclear explosion, both in size and mushroom-like form. The pyroclastic flow then ran down the mountainside at speeds exceeding one hundred miles per hour, leveling everything in its path for a distance of seventeen miles. Despite the devastation and tragedy wrought by the Mount St. Helens eruption, it was unquestionably the stuff movies are made of-which was precisely the thinking at Universal Pictures when the studio elected to bring its own fictionalization of the catastrophe to the big screen with Dante's Peak, a disaster epic produced by Gale Anne Hurd and Joseph M. Singer and directed by Roger Donaldson. Since Dante's Peak would require the replication of real-life events, familiarized through news broadcasts, Donaldson and his producers were intent upon signing a visual effects firm that could produce hyperrealistic, almost documentary-style volcanic simulations. Executive producer Ilona Herzberg had worked with Digital Domain during postproduction on Waterworld and had been impressed enough that she immediately thought of the facility when faced with the outrageous effects demands of Dante's Peak. "I took Roger Donaldson over to meet with them," Herzberg recalled, "and right away we realized that here was a studio big enough and diverse enough to handle all of our needs - everything from models to computer animation to practical effects." Reinforcing the assessment was the work Digital Domain had done on Apollo 13. That, more than anything, clinched the deal. Roger Donaldson - a geology enthusiast- initiated preproduction by delving into the science of volcanology and assembling a reel of authentic eruption footage for use as reference by himself and the effects team. "I did a lot of research because 62 - CINEFEX 69

I wanted to get the facts right," said Donaldson. "We employed three volcanologists to help us with the script and teach us how volcanologists operate: how they make their predictions, how accurate they are with those predictions, and what sort of pressures and dangers they face on the job. All of that information went towards making the movie as real as possible. Of course, the images were hyped somewhat- this was a movie, not a documentary - but the research enabled me to communicate to my crew the awesome scale of an eruption." Dante's Peak opens with a sequence in which volcanologist Harry Dalton (Pierce Brosnan) - stationed at a geological outpost in Colombia - loses his fiancee in the aftermath of a furious eruption. With that tragic back story established, the film jumps ahead four years to the sleepy mining town of Dante's Peak, where single mother and local businesswoman Rachel Wando (Linda Hamilton) serves as mayor. When a United States Geological Survey station picks up unusual seismic activity in the area, Harry and a team of field scientists are sent to survey the town's namesake mountain; and, after a series of investigative sojourns, the team confirms that Dante's Peak is a pot ready to boil. Before an evacuation can be ordered, however, all hell breaks loose on the mountain. Escape routes out of town are obstructed, and the residents of Dante's Peak find themselves pitted against the very worst nature has to offer: earthquakes and landslides, rivers of molten lava, raging firestorms and floodwaters, caustic ash and toxic gases- and a devastating pyroclastic flow. Enticed by the notion of creating - through digital or physical means - such epic-proportioned natural disasters, Digital Domain signed onto the project, with Patrick McClung agreeing to serve as visual effects supervisor. "As we began to review the boards," recalled effects executive producer Andrew Millstein, "we could see that this show was going to be a veritable melange of effects genres; and our biggest challenge, initially, was just figuring out the best effects method for each shot. As happens in Hollywood-with confounding regularity, it seems - another studio was engaged in mounting its own volcano project. After the framework was up, the mountain's rocky face was applied. "There are several ways to build a mountain," explained Alan Faucher. "The typical method is to cover the framework first with wire, then with screening material that is molded into the basic shape. Peter Hyams has built a career by making movies that tap into our most primal fears. To one degree or another, ilyams offerings such as Capricorn One, Outland and 2010 have all addressed the common dread of helplessness and isolation; and those same terrors are explored in the director's current film, The Relic. Set within a cavernous natural history museum, the movie pits a team of police and research scientists against a monster born of genetic mutation - a horrifically savage beast that feeds on man to survive. Dubbed a 'sophisticated haunted house movie' by producer Gale Anne Hurd, The Relic is also a good old-fashioned horror flick. "When people read the script, they thought it was Alien meets Jurassic Park," Hurd reflected. "That wasn't my thinking when it first came into my hands; but now that the movie's done and I've seen it on the screen, that seems like the perfect description. When we met early on, Peter and I shared the vision of this movie as one with suspense and thriller elements. But overall, it was simply something that is very unfashionable these days - a good horror movie. And I happen to love a good horror movie." Hyams was also a sucker for a solid scare: and the opportunity to make movie-goers jump out of their seats was among the temptations of the project. "In one way or another," Hyams remarked, "everybody is afraid of the dark. So the idea of being trapped in a confined space, in the dark, with something truly horrible, is terrifying." Hyams also relished the professional challenge of making a movie that was frightening, without descending into the ridiculous - a pitfall common to the genre. "I thought that if one could manage to make a film that was really scary, but at the same time was aiming to be intelligent, that would be the kind of film I would want to see. Unfortunately, only a few movies like that have been made - but those are the films that I truly admire." Among the scare films that fell under the heading of 'admirable' in Hyams' mind were Jaws, The Exorcist, Alien and the Hurd-produced Aliens. "I love Aliens - but it's a bit different from the others, because it's a film that tries to excite you more than terrify you. This time it's a war, versus, no one can hear you scream."" Hyams' intent was to bring something of both elements to The Relic, a creative goal that would, in part, rely on the effects support of Stan Winston Studio where the project's antagonist would be designed and realized. For digital and visual effects, Hyams turned to visual effects supervisor Greg McMurry of VIFX - a company that had collaborated with the director on previous projects - as well as Banned from the Ranch. During a ritualistic ceremony he is given a drug that acts like a virus, inserting its own genetic material into his cellular makeup and initiating his transformation into Kothoga, a horrific beast of mythological origin. However, he did have to be able to look behind himself and to raise his head up to stare down at his victims, the way a bear does when it's up on its hind legs." Using linear servo-powered mechanisms, Haugen designed elements of the creature performance that could be puppeteered in various combinations to achieve a broad range of movement. "The trickiest part of the mechanical design was getting the neck to move all the way up or all the way down without its mechanisms hitting the actor in the head." To lessen the burden for the performer within the suit, the mechanisms were milled out of aluminum, making the entire assembly a relatively lightweight thirty-five pounds. While the mechanical design was underway, the rest of the Winston crew proceeded with sculpting and molding the Kothoga suit. Two actors- Brian Steele and Vincent Hammondwere auditioned and cast as the Kothoga performers. Both had slim dancer's bodies and were about seven feet tall. "Contrary to what you'd expect," remarked Swift, "the actors didn't need to be bulky and big. They just needed to be tall and strong." To build up that strength, as well as learn to behave like the creature and walk on the extensions, the actors trained for three months with choreographer and behaviorist John Alexander, a veteran of Greystoke, Return to Oz and other projects showcasing actors in creature suits. A body cast to provide the basic form for sculpting the creature was done on Vincent Hammond, the taller of the two actors. Wearing a tight bodysuit, Hammond was placed on the limb extensions and directed to hold a neutral position while the Winston crew wrapped him in plaster bandages. "Since he had to stay in that position for several hours while the plaster dried," Chris Swift commented, "we placed him in a rig we had built that would help support his weight. We also saved the head for later so that he wouldn't have to endure having his entire body bandaged all at once." A fiberglass sculpting form was fashioned from Hammond's plaster bandage cast. This was then sectioned into various body parts to enable the Winston sculptors to work separately on a specific piece, then return it to its position in the whole to ensure the work was fitting appropriately. Because of the time crunch, the sculptors worked in water-based clay-easy to apply and sculpt - rather than oil-based clay. "The water-based clay was a problem in itself," Swift allowed, "because it always has to be covered and kept wet - otherwise it dries, cracks and, unlike oil-based clays, shrinks Wire applied to the surface of the fiberglass molds helped the clay to adhere. After the sculpture was finished, a syntactic mold was taken of all the separate pieces for the running of foam latex skin. Once applied to the core -which provided a basic form as well as a shell to surround the actor- the foam latex skin pieces were painted and hair was punched in along the creature's spine and scalp. Fangs and mandibles were modeled separately, then cast in rigid foam and skinned in polyurethane resin. Articulated front arms and rear legs completed the suit ensemble. In addition to the two articulated hero suits, a stunt suit was built for underwater scenes and a climactic scene in which the beast is set on fire. All three suits were wire-rigged to accommodate the long, catlike leaps required of the creature. Due to the squatting, allfours position of the performer inside, however, a standard flying harness could not be employed. "Ultimately," stated Swift, "we came up with a system that was based on a flight jacket. It

incorporated a customized set of pants that were connected to a harness with straps. A metal plate mounted to the back of the jacket held an interlocking bolt system for securing the actor to the suit." Getting either performer into the harnessed suit was a rigorous process. The suit was first hung in a semi-horizontal configuration. The actor climbed in through the creature's belly and got into the appropriate position. The suit was then lowered onto the actor's back until the plate on the jacket and the plate inside the suit were aligned. Next, the team climbed up ladders, opened a hatch in the back of the suit and helped the actor slip the suit bolt into the jacket lock. From the mechanical head, a power cable ran along the actor's back, out through an opening under Kothoga's tail. Arms and legs were finally attached, completing the lengthy process. Because suiting up was so arduous, once the actors were inside the suits they were required to remain in them throughout the shooting day. "Fans were installed to keep the actors cool," stated Haugen, "and fresh air was piped in via a third lung - kind of like the setup in a diving suit." On set, Kothoga was made to perform by whatever means a specific shot or scene required, either through radio-controlled puppeteering of the mechanical systems or through the actor's gross body movements. "Things you think are going to be easy often end up being very difficult," Winston noted, "and things you think are going to be impossible often turn out to be easy. In The Relic, there was a shot near the climax of the picture in which Kothoga has Penelope Ann Miller pinned up against a dumbwaiter-a fairly simple performance moment that only involved the head. But because of all the metal work around that part of the set, we had a horrible time with radio interference, and that created problems for the radio-control head. So this seemingly simple performance became difficult. On the other hand, shots I thought would be nearly impossible we got on the first take." A decision not to reveal the entire creature until the closing fifteen minutes of the movie contributed to the verisimilitude of the Kothoga performance. "The only way to scare people," Hyams said, "is to convince them that what they are seeing is real. And to do that, you have to be a bit of an illusionist. Like David Copperfield, my job was about misdirection and allowing the audience's imagination to play freely. Using Alien as a sort of matrix, I knew I had to be careful about how much I revealed of the creature, and when. I thought that when he was finally revealed, it should be sudden and it should be in the dark, leaving the audience to think, 'Oh my god, did I really see that?" Stan Winston Studio also supplied the production realisticlooking corpses representing Kothoga's victims. In total, four bodies and four decapitated heads were made by Richie Alonzo, Nick Marra, Chris Robbins and other members of the crew. To start the process, each of the actors playing the unfortunate victims was required to sit for a head casting: and one - whose character would undergo an autopsy in the film - had both his head and entire torso cast. "We used dental alginate for the casts," Alonzo stated, "which is a substance that dentists use to make impressions of teeth. Standard alginate is mixed with cold water, which would have been very uncomfortable for the actors- who had to be naked under the casts. To keep them from freezing, we had our alginate manufactured specially so that we could mix it up with warm water." After a cast had set, it was cut horizontally into two sections for removal, with any resulting damage immediately repaired. Attack wounds were then sculpted onto the surface. "For the autopsy body," said Alonzo, "we referred to a book we use often - The Atlas of Forensic Pathology - which has a lot of photographs of real accident victims. After a while, it gets a little disturbing to look at - but you just have to detach yourself and keep going." In addition to the atlas, a photograph of a real decapitation victim was located and used as reference in creating severe injuries such as jagged, torn skin fragments, a snapped spinal column and severed veins and muscles. From the completed sculptures, the Winston team molded replica bodies made of translucent silicone, a material closely resembling human flesh. The bodies were then painted - a task that was particularly arduous for the autopsy cadaver. "The autopsy body required tremendous detail," Alonzo related. "We built up layers of translucent silicone, painting between them so that the capillaries and veins would appear to lie just under the surface of the skin." In addition to the horrid wounds that had been sculpted onto the body, the artists painted in bruises and small scratches to simulate the look of a person who has suffered an animal attack. "Between the painted detail, which made the body look real, and the flesh-like translucent silicone, which made the body feel real, the autopsy cadaver was a double whammy for the actress portraying the coroner-and everyone else. Everybody on the set was wincing when we shot that scene." The ultimate compliment to the team's artistry came from Peter Hyams, who had reservations about shooting the autopsy scene too explicitly once he actually had the body on the set. "Peter thought the body was too real looking. He was concerned that if he shot it the way he originally intended to, he wouldn't be able to get the movie rating he was going for. So he wound up sort of shooting around it" Absolute realism was mandated for the decapitated heads, since each would have to capture precisely the facial features of the actor playing the victim. Silicone heads, created from the actors' lifecasts, were painstakingly airbrushed, with reference photographs used to recreate every vein, discoloration and spot on the actor's face in paint. The painted heads were then delivered to Stuart Artingstall's hair department, where hair was hand-punched into the silicone scalps one strand at a time. Eyes made of dental acrylic were also produced in-house, then painted to match each actor's eye color and coated with clear acrylic to create a natural sheen. Digital effects supervisor John DesJardin initiated the CG creature assignment by guiding research into a software regimen that would allow the VIFX team to model, animate and render the character. "To prepare for this project," DesJardin recalled, "I was given two months and a small team of researchers. "We would animate skeletons in Softimage, create skin deformation - such as the wiggle and jiggle of flesh and muscles - in Alias/Wavefront, and render in RenderMan, with Prisms doing the interface between all of the separate packages. It seemed nightmarish at first, but we were able to develop the glue to stick it all together, and we ended up with a very efficient production channel." Even with a game plan established, however, the system required a lot of tweaking in order to get the separate programs to talk to each other. "If I animated the movement of an arm in Softimage," DesJardin explained, "and then imported that animation into Alias/Wavefront, Alias would read it in a weird way due to the different ways Softimage and Alias run their inverse kinematics systems." To get the two to agree, the team wrote a program that translated the Softimage data for Alias. "I gave the team the assignment of writing predetermined connec tions between muscle and bone movement. If the bones of an arm were animated in Softimage, Alias would reinterpret how the bones moved - and then correctly interpret how the muscle movement of the arm should look. Once both the background and greenscreen elements were scanned, Dietrich was able to rough in simple choreography of the creature and a digital version of the officer, adding more detail with each subsequent animation pass. "To create the digital cop," said Dietrich, "we actually scanned in the actor wearing his police costume. But the real challenge was working on the animation to transition between the real actor and the digital one, trying to create realistic motion throughout." but also how much blood would be generated by such a violent act. "To build the cast," related Schneider, "I mixed plaster with stearic acid, which made it rigid and brittle. Then I laid about a half inch of clay into the mold and backed that with urethane. Fresh from their work on Congo and Twister, graphics producer Casey Cannon and designer/supervisor Van Ling set about the task of creating a digital character of their own, albeit one that stayed in the computer. "Usually what is seen on a computer monitor in movies is created through video playback," Ling explained. "The video runs and the actors look at a fake computer monitor and pretend they are typing on a fake keyboard. But because computers are more and more a part of our lives, the computer in a movie now has to become a character itself, something that we really believe." In The Relic, a computer called the Interpolator is used to ascertain the physiological and genetic makeup of the Kothoga creature. Ostensibly created by Margo Green, the Interpolator analyzes the DNA chain of a specimen and compares it to all known DNA chains in order to identify the family, genus and species for that particular animal. "In reality," Ling explained, "limited versions of such systems do exist - but they required hundreds of computers that have to crunch numbers for days or weeks to come up with a solution. Even then, their findings will be incomplete, because not all DNA data for every animal on earth has been catalogued. But in the fictional world of The Relic, one computer does the entire job." Banned from the Ranch was engaged to produce the Interpolator software that would be featured in the picture, along with a labful of other DNA analysis computer graphics. Determined to base the system on reality, Ling and his team picked the brains of a number of geneticists and molecular biologists for how their 'wish list' software system might actually work, and also contacted Perkin-Elmer Corporation, an actual manufacturer of genetic analysis hardware. In a product placement agreement with Paramount, Perkin-Elmer provided a number of authentic genetic analysis workstations for use on the set. "The system is designed so that a sample of DNA can be applied, along with chemical reagents that will multiply the DNA for analysis," Ling explained. "Other enzymes cut the DNA and start chain reactions. The idea behind the Interpolator in the movie is that all of that information goes directly into Green's computer. She supposedly loads the data, and then the Interpolator figures out what it is." Shots of the Interpolator at work reveal on-screen computer graphics that incorporate DNA gel images recognizable to any biochemist. In the sequence, these images flip through the screen, like cherries on a slot machine, as the system attempts to find possible matches. To create those images on various monitors throughout the set, Banned from the Ranch artists employed a combination of graphics and animation software packages, including Adobe Photoshop, Electric Image and inhouse, custom programs. "The great thing about the way we were able to create the program was that Penelope Ann Miller could act with the computer. Instead of having to time her performance to a set video playback, she had control keys that allowed her to change the images on the screens whenever she was ready. As long as she hit the right keys, the results she was looking for would come up. We also had the ability to create or reprogram graphics on the set, to allow Peter and the actors total flexibility. In one instance, we were able to program some of James Whitmore's more technical dialogue into a graphic, like a cue card." Before running the programs on set, however, Ling and his crew did a test shoot, with Peter Hyams there to film the monitors and ensure the graphics were reading properly on film. "At the beginning of every show," said Ling, "we do test shots on our monitors, running our software. We set up three computers, each with a different color temperature. Peter was able to look at them through playback and tell us exactly how to adjust them, which allowed for extra comfort once we got to the set. He knew going in that he didn't have to worry about how blue or how red the monitors would appear, because they were all preset to work with his lighting and filters." The skill and professionalism exhibited by all three of The Relic's effects teams helped to put the horror in Peter Hyams' good old-fashioned horror movie. "Making movies is about being better than you are," Hyams reflected. "It's like trying to pour a quart of water into a pint bottle - and that's where folks like Stan Winston and the teams at VIFX and Banned from the Ranch come in. There is something so wonderful about working with them, you want them to be pleased with what you've done as a director. In a way, the energy that comes from those shops is the real essence of movie-making. It's a whole bunch of people sitting around saying, 'My father has a barn -we could put on a play!' PHOENIX RISING article by Kevin H. Martin

Over the past three decades, the Star Trek universe has developed a densely detailed and thoroughly comprehensive back story - comprising plots from four live-action television series, seven feature films, hundreds of published novels and comics and select elements from a mid-seventies cartoon adaptation. With the Star Trek phenomena explored by so many ancillary avenues, a determination finally had to be made as to which of the depicted events were, in fact, canonical; and, after some deliberation, it was decided that only the aforementioned television and film installments were 'true' Star Trek history. In 1994, Star Trek Generations attempted to bridge the gap in this established chronology by resolving the fate of the original Star Trek's Captain James I. Kirk while introducing the crew of The Next Generation television series to the big screen. For its follow-up, Star Trek: First Contact, a decision was made to reemploy the long-running series' most formidable villains - flesh-and-metal hybrid conquerors, called the Borg, Introduced in a 1989 episode, the Borg were featured only sparingly thereafter, in a scant six additional episodes- an admirable show of restraint that permitted the characters to retain their menace and kept them from becoming commonplace baddies. Bringing the Borg into play for First Contact was a strategy akin to the successful use of Khan in Star Trek II- reintroduce a previously established, fan-popular antagonist, against which the starship veterans could shine in battle. First Contacts storyline would draw upon an event in Star Trek history that was also well established, although never before depicted. The original television show had laid the groundwork with a back story concerning the inventor of mankind's first successful warp drive, Zefram Cochrane - a role essayed by Glenn Corbett in the series, but played by James Cromwell in the new film. Cochrane's historic warp drive flight was a seminal event, since it led to man's colonization of the stars and, a century later, the establishment of the United Federation of Planets. The sequel would take that back story further, linking it to an event undocumented in the approved Star Trek canon: first contact with an alien species. After helming several Next Generation television episodes, series costar Jonathan Frakes -Commander Will Riker - was signed to direct the Paramount franchise's eighth feature film, following in the crossover paths previously tread by Leonard Nimoy and William Shatner. Fresh from directing a CD-ROM adventure showcasing the Klingons, Frakes began by immersing himself in aspects of the production relating to the story-a Terminator-ish tale of the Borg going back in time to change history and prevent the establishment of the Federation. Series executive producer Rick Berman and associate producer Peter Lauritson reprised their roles as overseers of the film's effects and conceptual efforts, assembling a team of artisans from within the ranks of past and present Star Trek outings, both on television and on the big screen. Production designer Herman Zimmerman and many of his regular art department contributors - including graphic designers Michael and Denise Okuda and conceptual artists Ricardo Delgado, Rick Sternbach and John Eaves - would create environments for both the 21st and 24th centuries, as well as design a brand-new starship Enterprise. Berman and Lauritson chose series coordinator David Takemura to supervise the overall effects thrust, which entailed garnering the cooperation of a variety of Star Trek-savvy effects houses. Industrial Light & Magic-under returning supervisor John Knoll and first-time effects producer Jeff Olson -would produce, through stage and digital means, the majority of the space segments, including depictions of the Enterprise, Scott Rader and Adam Howard - Emmy Award-winning visual effects supervisors who had overseen effects for all three Star Trek series, formerly at Digital Magic and currently at Pacific Ocean Post-were charged with a diverse CG, animation and compositing assignment. VisionArt supervisor Josh Rose and team would follow up their creation of a virtual fleet of CG spaceships for Deep Space Nine's revised title sequence with the rendering of a Vulcan starship featured at the film's conclusion. Digital matte artistry would be supplied by Star Trek veterans at Matte World Digital and Illusion Arts; and special effects supervisor Terry Frazee would return to provide a blend of pyrotechnic and physical stage effects. Once the script was submitted to ILM, Knoll and Olson concentrated on dividing the workload - particularly shots of the Enterprise and other featured starships - between motion control stages and the digital realm. "If one of the ships was to be seen full-screen and at length," explained associate visual effects supervisor George Murphy, "we knew it would be done as a stage model. Ships that would be doing a lot of elaborate maneuvers in space battle scenes would be created digitally." Even with the game plan established, ILM's work was delayed as Paramount settled on the visual identity of the new Enterprise. Neither the digital nor the physical stage models could be constructed until that design issue was settled. "We were fully a third of the way into this project before we saw a finalized Enterprise design," related Olson. "We couldn't build our physical model until we had an approved design and construction blueprints; and we couldn't build our CG version until we had the physical miniature built." To make good use of time, despite the delay, Knoll had ILM art director Alex Jaeger begin work on a series of animatics for the Star Wars-style space battle that occurs early in the film. Jaeger also started designs on four new classes of Federation starship-all digital models - that would appear in the battle. "Paramount wanted us to expand on the Star Trek universe," Jaeger recalled, "presenting kinds of starships no one had seen before. Initially, they wanted a dozen new starships, so I did about eighteen designs. But once they realized what it would cost to build and texture all of these different CG models, they whittled it down to four ships really fast." Visual diversity was important in the starship designs, not only to broaden the established Star Trek ship style, but to ensure that audiences would not mistake any of the battling federation starships for the Enterprise. "They had to look quite distinct, which meant that I was allowed to vary the designs quite a bit." Star Trek: First Contact begins, uncharacteristically, with nightmare imagery - a hellish recollection by Enterprise Captain Jean-Luc Picard (Patrick Stewart) of his temporary assimilation by the Borg years earlier. Illusion Arts was instrumental in creating a spectacular opening pullback, which begins tight on the left eye of Picard, who is locked, Borg-like, into a modular cell. "A black field with some amorphous swirls and shapes - which might be nebulae or interstellar gas clouds - turns out to be the iris of Picard's eye as the pullback begins," explained Illusion Arts co-founder Bill Taylor. "By starting the shot at a microscopically small level, we let the audience guess what it is they're seeing." As the pullback continues, Picard's cell is revealed as just one of many such borg-filled units. To capture the tighter cell images, Stewart was filmed on a hundred-footlong, rectangular stage set, designed by Herman Zimmerman and the studio art department. Individual cells were equipped with circular monitors, life-support units and communication equipment. Both Picard and the live-action element become minuscule images on screen as the camera recedes even further, revealing thousands of housing units within the monumental, cube-shaped Borg vessel. In more than one sense, the initial concept for the shot revisited old territory. Illusion Arts had done a similar dramatic pullback within the cube ship for the 1989 television episode, using miniature foreground elements to enhance a multiplane matte painting. "Our original instructions were to redo what we had created for the series," recalled Taylor. "They asked for 'the same, only more so.'" To start, Taylor's partner, Syd Dutton, made the decision to have Robert Stromberg and Mike Wassel- two artists at Illusion Arts - develop concepts for the Borg ship interior simultaneously. Dutton himself had found inspiration in a book on 19th-century architecture. "There was a photograph that 1 admired of the enormous cast-iron structure used in building the Kew Botanical Gardens in 1845," Dutton said. "It occurred to me that the pattern of shapes in that could be adapted to the Borg vessel interior. So I suggested to Robert Stromberg that he scan a portion of the photo and play with it." Stromberg, whose paintings had played a pivotal role in defining the look of alien environments in the television series, ultimately cre-ated a digital painting in which the units of Zimmerman's set were replicated in every direction. At the same time, Mike Wassel was developing an alternative concept for the Borg interior, starting with a torus defined in StrataPro which he rendered and then used as the basis for a painting. When the two concepts were presented to Berman, the decision was made to incorporate both into the pullback.
