The first third of the 35-second pullback contains live-action elements filmed in Vistavision by Bill Taylor on stage at Paramount. Two separate shots- a 50mm macro-lens closeup of Picard's eye that pulls back to a medium shot, and a second 35mm lens pullback that reveals the entire set - were digitally blended to make them appear as one uninterrupted camera move. One of the problems in tying the two shots together was the fact that the best frames for matching the overall move were not the best frames for matching the perspective on Picard's face. To solve the problem, Picard's head in the wider shot was replaced with his head from the previous shot. The tracking, stabilizing and compositing of the two images, by Ken Nakada and Richard Patterson, was accomplished using After Effects software on Macintoshes. The remainder of the shot is entirely computer generated. Depth was added to Stromberg's painting by splitting it into separate planes and then executing a camera move in Electric Image. Another segment of the shot was enhanced with a tunnel, created as a 3-D computer model by Fumi Mashimo, using textures painted by Stromberg. For the final segment, Mashimo recreated Wassel's toroidal shape in Form-Z and used Electric Image to 'camera map' Wassel's painting onto the geometry. "Camera mapping is the reverse of texture mapping," Mashimo explained. "Normally, it is very difficult to paint a texture map, because you have to paint on a flattened surface; so you can't really see where you are on the object while you're painting. Surface areas get distorted in the same way a globe is distorted when it is turned into a flat, rectangular wall map. With camera mapping, you can start with a shape, enter a single view of it and paint on that view. Electric Image then strips the skin off the view you have painted and generates the flat texture map that can be put back onto the object in the proper perspective as the camera moves. There are limits to how far off axis you can move the camera, of course, but it's a very efficient tool for a pullback like this." Mashimo also added 3-D cables hanging from above camera to enhance the sense of movement through space, then created a single move in Electric Image to tie all of the elements together. Atmospheric effects rendered separately contributed to the sense of scale. Concerned about the illogic of toroidal chambers inside a ship with a cube-shaped exterior, Rick Berman asked Illusion Arts to render a second version with rectangular walls outside the curved shapes; but after seeing the alternate version, he agreed that the first was better, and the original concept was approved. As to the inconsistency between the ship's interior and exterior - a detail that ultra-observant Star Trek fans were sure to notice - Berman's solution was to 'let 'em wonder.' Inconsistencies with the previously established look of the Borg themselves were not a problem, as the creatures' original design had never been intended for verbatim translation to the big screen. In fact, early production reports made note of discussions with H.R. Giger concerning a Borg redesign; and although Giger and the studio never agreed to terms, some of the artist's biomechanically-flavored influence did color the design process. Conceptual artist Ricardo Delgado, brought on board the project at the behest of Zimmerman, proceeded to design new Borg creatures that suggested powerful, beetle-like, hard-shelled insects. Delgado's prime directive was to spruce up the Borg. "I took that to mean giving their shapes some power," Delgado commented, "especially their profiles, which sometimes looked too busy on TV. Rather than emphasize odd little details, I wanted to amplify the sense of strength in each Borg. Everybody agreed that we needed to take them to the nth degree - it was just a matter of settling on what constituted the nth degree." One of the details established in the television series was the Borg logo - but Delgado opted to steer well clear of that somewhat preposterous idea. "The Borg know who they are - they don't need a logo to advertise it. for television continuity, that kind of thing is fine; but it would only have taken away from their menace if we'd brought that to the fore in the film. Instead, I focused on the contrasts and textures inherent in the elemental Borg design. The quintessential Borg elements are patterns upon patterns, shapes atop shapes and flesh atop circuitry atop flesh." Bringing the Borg minions to life fell to Michael Westmore and his makeup crew, who created every Borg head seen in the film, basing their work on a Delgado design that had met with the producers' approval. "Our principal directive for the Borg heads," Westmore explained, "was to take them from the pale zombie look they'd had on television to something that had some depth, with marbleization and luminosity. For the television series, we had just made latex helmets - but that was because we needed to grind out a bunch of them quickly. For the film, we wanted to see the actual skin and how the mechanical pieces pierced the flesh." The Borg head makeups consisted of both appliances to suggest mechanical implants and organic-looking facial prosthetics, all of which were sculpted by Jake Garber, whom Westmore recruited specifically for the First Contact project. "Jake also sculpted an appliance for the armature that pops out of Picard's face during his assimilation nightmare," Westmore remarked. "The actual popping out was a CG effect; but Jake's appliance was used for the end of the shot. That same armature piece was used on other Borg characters as well." Borg eyepieces were sculpted by Barry Koper, while Westmore's son engineered the blinking eyelights. "Michael Jr. had created Geordi's head blinkies at the start of the series," Westmore commented, "so we've always turned to him whenever we've had to go into somebody's head with electronics. Altogether, we made up thirty-six eye pieces, some with blinkies, some with lasers - and every one of them blinks out a name in Morse code. Anyone in the audience who knows Morse would recognize names of studio executives, technicians - even my son's dog."

One of the challenges of the Borg makeup assignment was to create the illusion that hundreds of Borg were inhabiting the Enterprise when, in reality, only eight actors were engaged to portray the Borg multitude. "Fortunately," said Westmore, "the appliances had been sculpted in such a way that they could be easily modified and added to; and as the film progressed, my artist became more and more adept at doing that. We would turn the appliances upside down or backward to create an entirely new look on the same performer. Although there were just two primary wraparound mechanical devices for the head, all of the other pieces could be customized in this fashion - and that gave us a lot of flexibility." Such flexibility was even more of an issue since the movie would feature never-beforeseen alien Borg hybrids, "We had Klingon Borg, Romulan Borg, Bolian Borg, and even a Cardassian Borg." Hired to construct the Borg suits was Todd Masters Company, whose alien concepts had illuminated NBC's Dark Skies, and with whom Michael Westmore had worked previously on the Voyager series. Masters was provided with costuming concepts - devised by designer Deborah Everton - that were much more sophisticated than the black longjohns tricked out with transistor radio pieces seen in the television episodes. "Deborah's illustrations went well beyond that," Masters noted, "and she had created a look we really liked. We interpreted her illustrations to create a series of maquettes; then she worked with us to get these models to the point where production would sign off on them and we could start building the costumes full-size. We scanned the maquettes into the computer and I proceeded to paint the suit, testing a variety of colors. Rick Berman wanted these Borg to be dramatically different visually from what had been seen on television; so, instead of all-black costumes with a bit of gray thrown in, these Borg colors included coppers and golds and high-intensity chromes. When we had finished painting the Borg suits, we compared them against stills of the sets to make sure they fit in with Herman Zimmerman's overall color scheme." Masters was also engaged to construct custom mechanical appendages for the Borg characters. As established in previous incarnations, most Borg are equipped with unique tool arms - a drill press on one, a circular saw on another - and Masters spent weeks drafting variations on that idea. Restricted by a limited budget, however, he and his crew could manufacture only a few 'A-level' arms-servo-articulated, robotic devices for use in closeups and other foreground shots- while many simple background arms were built. Both versions were fitted onto the baker's dozen of complete Borg suits fashioned to stand in for the many thousand members of the collective. For an opening flashback featuring Picard as Locutus, speaker for the Borg collective, Masters was given only the remains of the Borg outfit last worn by Patrick Stewart for the premiere episode of Deep Space Nine. "It had galoshes and phone cords on the feet," Masters said, "and underwear sprinkled with polyfoam and model parts. It looked bad, and there was no budget to upgrade it. But this was for the first shot in the movie; and we knew that the fans would feel cheated if Patrick was wearing this rag while all the other Borg looked great - so we punched it up at our own expense." Aping a current trend in horror films, Picard appears to wake up from his flashback nightmare, but finds he is still dreaming as a Borg servo unit pops out of his cheek like a mechanical flower. The effect had been conceived originally as a physical gag, but was ultimately rendered digitally by Stephen Braggs at ILM. Picard finally wakes from his nightmare, from which he derives an ominous portent - the Borg are returning. His premonition is confirmed when a message from Starfleet Command warns of a massive cube-shaped ship detected on a course for earth. Considered a security risk by his superiors -and thus denied permission to join the battle fleet being assembled to face the Borg - Picard nonetheless orders the Enterprise E into warp drive and heads straight for the conflict. Conceived as the most powerful Enterprise ever, the Enterprise E-a new class of starship- would be an amalgamation of previous starships, yet still make its own visual statement. "It is more streamlined and graceful than the other starships," observed ILM model shop supervisor John Goodson. "It always looks as if it is in motion, even while at rest." The new starship was designed principally by conceptual artist John Eaves, who began working on its exterior with Herman Zimmerman four months prior to shooting, although he had been considering new starship designs since refurbishing the Excelsior to become the Enterprise B for Star Trek Generations. "My main goal," Eaves stated, "was to come up with a sleek model that would look good from all angles so there'd be a lot of flexibility in shooting it." One way in which the completed ship differed from the Enterprise D featured on the current Voyager series was the length of the engine nacelles. "We decided this was a different engine type - faster, yet longer-lived - and the longer length of the engines helped to create the desired sleekness." Working by hand rather than computer, Eaves developed the new vessel over three conceptual passes, then secured approval from Rick Berman before passing on the design to Rick Sternbach for blueprinting. Fabricating the ten-foot motion control model -which represented a vessel approximately 2500 feet in length - was a short-duration, but labor-intensive procedure. The model was armatured to handle eight mounts; and Jon Foreman installed electrical plugs at each of those points, allowing for quick changes on the internal lighting. In filming the model, effects director of photography Marty Rosenberg was challenged by the artistic decision to spotlight areas on the starship, emphasizing the self-lit, ocean-liner-atsea vision devised by Douglas Trumbull for the first widescreen Enterprise voyage. In later films, ILM had retained the effectfaked with off-camera lights cast from a moving rig - but the Generations ship was without these 'logo lights. For the new film, a heavy-duty model mount permitted rolling and moving spotlight setups that sustained the illusion of a gloriously selfilluminating ship. To create glowing warp engines, the nacelle caps on the model were internally equipped with the equivalent of pulsating disco balls. An animatic, choreographed by Alex Jaeger, served as a precise reference for the new vessel's on-screen debut, and was translated faithfully when Rosenberg executed his motion control photography. The initial plan for shooting various views of the ship in deep space had been to reproduce the Generations lighting scheme - highlight-enhancing rim light, plus a relatively dark fill. The lighting scheme was altered, however, when Paramount - after viewing several shots of the new Enterprise - requested additional fill light. Further illumination was provided via backlit transparencies mounted behind the model's tiny windows. Knoll had wanted to implement the window gag for Generations, but the requisite budget for such an approach had not been available. "We decided to try it this time out," remarked Goodson. "We cut sixteenth-inch frames for each window, bending them to fit the curve of the hull before gluing and sanding them flush. A laser-cut plex window lens went in, backed with peel-off paper facing outward. Then, behind the plex we mounted quarter-inch-thick acrylic blocks with photographic slides and diffusion glued onto them. The internal illumination fit right behind this sandwich, giving us a little neon lightbox." After the model was painted, the paper covering the windows was peeled away, revealing backlit images of actual sets, provided by Paramount. Although sufficient for the smaller windows, the transparency gag would not work for two larger groups of windows in the saucer. One revealed a conference room that had to match up with a live-action set constructed at Paramount. "We filled that area of the model with tiny, micro-scale furniture," Goodson elaborated, "including tables and chairs." Other windows requiring actual miniature sets were situated on the backside of the ship's dish, where a miniature arboretum - complete with trees and bottom-lit pools of water - was featured. "That tied in with the Enterprise in the original movie, which had an arboretum down in the secondary hull." The Enterprise E is first spotted as it passes within the body of a gaseous nebula. "The producers were specific in wanting to see a passage through stellar phenomena," remarked George Murphy. "The ship is, at first, partially obscured by foreground extensions of gas clouds; but as it exits the nebula and makes a big turn towards camera, it grows progressively more visible." While the shot was realized, in part, through model photography of the ship, the nebula was created digitally by computer graphics supervisor Habib Zargarpour, technical directors Joakim Arnesson and Marc Cooper, compositor Tim Alexander and digital matte artist Brian Flora. After reviewing deep space photography captured by the orbiting Hubble telescope, Arnesson employed a combination of 2-D art and 3-D particle rendering. "While the background nebula was flat, the foreground needed genuine 3-D parallax as the Enterprise came out of this dark matter and soared up past camera," related Zargarpour. "It was a reasonable approach to combine a multiplane background with a volumetric foreground." While no starship leaves the Paramount film dock without transporter and warp drive effects, this voyage would streamline the process. After being altered for the last feature, the transporter effect was returned to the style established on The Next Generation TV series. At Pacific Ocean Post, Adam Howard and Scott Rader- each of whom had wrangled with the beamins and beam-outs on The Next Generation, Deep Space Nine and Voyager-were responsible for the transporter effect encore. Entirely unchanged was the warp speed effect - executed by John Knoll - in which the starship stretches, and then vanishes in a starburst. As the Enterprise warp-speeds homeward, a fleet of wouldbe defenders encounters the Borg ship- a two-mile-long cube in space that is decidedly nonaerodynamic in appearance. The limited angles and specific lighting required to make a cubeshaped model read properly had proved vexing from the time the ship made its television debut. In fact, striking storyboard art and elaborate battle choreography for a two-part Borg TV episode had been summarily jettisoned when series effects supervisor Rob Legato fully realized the limitations of the hastily assembled cube model. Frustrated, Legato had settled for a mix of static shots and straightforward flybys of the ship. The cubed design proved just as unworkable for the feature film. "We reviewed shots of the cube from the series," Goodson remarked, "and were acutely aware of its limitations." Clearly, an all-new Borg ship was required. Two early ship concepts deviated from the previously seen Borg cube. The first, a tetrahedron - a solid shape with four triangular surfaces- was dropped due to the shape's inherent lack of visual impact and excitement, especially when photographed from low angles. A second concept - also dismissed - involved an entire squadron of Borg vessels arranged in perfect formation to create a single ship. "It was like a Borg latticework that worked as one and moved as one," explained George Murphy. "It would have made for a really nice visual - but it diminished the Borg villains to suggest they needed this many ships to beat Starfleet." Ultimately, the concept of a cube-shaped ship was revived - although a new model, measuring thirty inches to a side and including a wealth of detail, was created. Bill George - who had

served as an art director on previous Star Trek features and was engaged as a consultant for First Contact - suggested specific, more interesting textures, achievable as photo-etched brass "There were layers and layers of detail," observed Alex Jaeger, "five inches deep, which helped convey the complexity and scale of this ship." Internal neon illumination was broken up by a patterned, eighteen-inch lightbox to suggest many different compartments and light sources within the model. Opening fire on the Borg cube, the Starfleet defenders make impact, but fail to inflict lethal damage. The attack was simulated, in part, through the laying of miniature pyrotechnic elements. "Our pyro crew did a lot of work for this show," Jaeger confirmed. "They blew up several black cubes packed with debris, and we were able to match up those blast elements to our model photography." During the compositing, explosions were colored green to coordinate with the Borg ship's interior and exterior color motif. Damage to the alien craft was suggested by the removal of specific model sections, with a burn then airbrushed around the 'damaged' area. Of the Starfleet vessels engaged in the space battle, only the Farragut and the Enterprise were models filmed on stage. The other starships - including the Defiant, commanded by Worfwere achieved digitally. "We could have shot the existing Defiantstage model," John Knoll acknowledged, "which we had on hand for the crew to use as reference. But with the short production schedule, there was a limit to the amount of time we'd have on the motion control stages. It was a more efficient distribution of our resources to do that ship in CG." Since VisionArt had already created a very credible CG model of the Defiant for its numerous appearances on Deep Space Nine, Knoll obtained the company's modeling data, onto which new textures - based on transparencies taken of the three-foot miniature - were mapped. Other CG ships featured in the sequence were an Akira-class vessel with a catamaran body, a Sabre-class ship, a Norway-class in the tradition of TV's Voyager, and a Steamrunner-class ship with saucer-mounted cowlings into which the engine nacelles nestled. The intricate battle choreography of the ships was worked out by Stu Maschwitz, an animator who had revealed an innate talent for aerial maneuvering in the Mission: Impossible helicopter sequences. "Those same kinds of dynamics and motions were needed for this scene," noted George Murphy, "so we relied on Stu to tackle the battle choreography. He also came up with some nicely finessed bits of business for the background ships. The dogfight turned out to be a little bit Star Wars, a little bit Top Gun; and it was much faster than the battles in the earlier Star Trek features." The mostly digital fleet has been nearly routed by the single Borg cube by the time Picard and company arrive on the scene. The look of battle damage on the CG ships was a concern to John Knoll. "I was fairly satisfied with the CG damage seen in Generations," Knoll said, "which was pretty much just painted black markings and scorching. But this time, I had Alex Jaeger start with practical materials in order to create those elements. He took sheet metal and blasted it with a torch; then he tried all kinds of other materials to get a variety of detailed and realistic burn marks that we could use as textures on the CG models." Using sense memory of his Borg experience, Picard directs the beleaguered battle fleet to focus its firepower on a specific area of the Borg cube, resulting in the ship's destruction. Just prior to the fatal Starfleet assault, however, the Borg manage to escape, emerging from the ship in a giant sphere - represented by a two-foot-diameter model, built and photographed by ILM. "We vacuformed about fifteen different patterns that conformed to this spherical curve," noted Goodson, "and covered those with a lot of molded and cast pieces. Then we added tons of acid-etched brass over it, just like we had on the cube." For the initial shot of the sphere actually rising from the Borg ship, the miniature - built at a larger scale than the thirty-inch cube model -was filmed separately. That motion control photography was then composited into footage of the cube model, which had been fabricated with an articulated, five-inch-long, motion-controlled passageway specifically for the scene of the sphere exiting the ship. After rescuing Worf from the battle-damaged Defiant, Picard pursues the escaping Borg, tracking the earthward movement of the sphere on the Enterprise's main viewscreen. The bridge monitor - a mainstay of all past starships - differed somewhat from its predecessors. "This viewscreen is supposed to be a holographic projection," explained Jaeger, "as opposed to just a flat unit on the wall." To simulate the holographic view, 3-D computer generated imagery was composited into live-action photography of the bridge. Rick Rische created moving sky elements for each shot, while Paul Rivera acted as chief digital compositor, utilizing patches to glue elements of the plate back together after they had been repositioned to best effect. After Matte World Digital had worked its magic on the backgrounds, the plates were returned to VisionArt, where the descending CG Vulcan ship was added. A different approach was taken for shots of the ship already on the ground, with Rose's crew adding their digital spaceship prior to transmitting the plates to Matte World Digital - in part, so that they could finesse the ship's positioning in the plate before matte painted elements were added. "We had to cheat the scale on the ship from one shot to the next, Rose explained, "in order to make it seem to fit into this too-small clearing. There were weird parallax problems feeding into the lens of the plate camera - an unusually high degree of curvature - plus problems just being able to see enough of the ship, given the theoretical distance between the camera and the vessel." The back-and-forth working relationship between VisionArt and Matte World Digital was facilitated by communication directly through the Internet. "It turned out to be a terrific aid,"

Evans elaborated, "a way to clarify problems and really speed the process along, while actually transferring elements over the Net, and then recombining them. The file formats were alldigital data, and we used an ISDN line to bring the elements into our workstations." With contact established between humans and Vulcans, the Enterprise departs for the 24th century, reentering the temporal vortex and vanishing into the night sky as the 21st-century earthlings watch in awe. Although little detail was needed for the digital element of the distant ship-seen from the earth as a small dot in the sky - some digital tweaking was required to make the live-action night sky more closely match the Matte World Digital renderings that precede and follow the shot. The film's conclusion begins with a 91-second match-move pullback that originates with the Vulcan-to-human first contact scene on the ground. "A Vistavision crane shot was filmed on location rising up and pulling back for the last scene of the film," stated Barron. "The pullback scene was reduced and extended over the length of the shot by combining it with motion control photography of a miniature clearing and surrounding landscape. The elements were then combined, using motion tracking code written by Chris Horvath in Alias/Wavefront Composer. Ken Evans and Susumu Yunuhiro built the landscape, with fiftieth-scale trees; then Cameron Noble, assisted by Todd R. Smith, shot the miniature for us in Vistavision. It was hard work to duplicate the pine needles and get a texture that would photograph properly: but when it was completed, it was an impressive sight." A painting by Caroleen Green served as a scenic backing for the miniature. While certainly not the final Star Trek chapter, First Contact did serve to resolve some of the tangled story threads of the ongoing saga - and, before it was finished, the movie had spun a production history that was nearly as convoluted. In evaluating that history, Jeff Olson stands amazed at the differences between ILM's originally contracted assignment and the number and complexity of the shots actually produced. "It's like an entirely different show," Olson commented, "at least in terms of volume. All of the same sequences are there - but in an expanded form, with many more shots. That was a big part of the challenge of getting Star Trek: First Contact up to the level on which it had to operate - as a thrilling, occasionally shocking modern movie. Like the Borg, motion pictures have expanded and intensified to the point where they grab you by the throat and assimilate you." CRASH McCREERY DOING DINOSAURS AND SUCH article by John Shannon As a talented artist and child fascinated with all things fantastic, Mark 'Crash' McCreery made the proclamation that, when he grew up, he was going to 'do dinosaurs. Years later, as a designer and illustrator for Stan Winston Studio, he found himself doing just that when Winston assigned him to a project in development at Universal entitled Jurassic Park. "I had no idea what 'do dinosaurs' meant," McCreery stated. "I didn't know in what capacity I might be doing dinosaurs. I just knew that I wanted to be a part of that world. I used to draw little landscapes and put all of my dinosaurs into them, just to imagine what kind of world they lived in. I loved monster movies; but dinosaurs were even better because they actually existed. I'm still fascinated by that. I look at the head of a T-rex, which is the scariest thing in the world, and I am fascinated by the fact that this animal lived and breathed and walked the earth." Born to an Air Force family in Colorado Springs, Colorado, McCreery spent his early childhood in the vagabond style of military life. When he was ten, his father retired, and the nomadic McCreerys settled in San Luis Obispo, California, where they indulged their individual interests in art and nature. "The whole household had an artistic flow to it," said McCreery. "My mother is an excellent painter, and my older brother and two sisters are all artistically inclined. My family was also very outdoor-oriented, constantly going on camping trips and hikes; and I think that bred a deep appreciation for nature. That was the kind of thing I liked to draw when I was young - animals and birds, especially birds of prey. I think most of my training came from observing nature. Before I ever went to art school and studied anatomy and all of those technical things you have to learn, I seemed to have an understanding of light and shade, the natural order of things, how things relate to each other. I think that came Stan Winston Studio conceptual artist Mark 'Crash' McCreery at work on a pterodactyl illustration for The Lost World. from the fact that my family was very in tune with nature and our surroundings." McCreery also found himself drawn to movies, particularly those in the science fiction and horror genres. "King Kong and The Creature From the Black Lagoon were two films that hooked me. And I made it my business to learn about stop-motion and Ray Harryhausen and Willis O'Brien. A favorite magazine was Creepy, whose covers were often graced with illustrations by Frank Frazetta. "Frank Frazetta was probably my biggest influence. His paintings captured a certain essence of story. As a kid, I found myself sucked into the story behind the paintings. It was as if he had caught something in the process of motion, and I really wanted to see what was going to happen next. That's why I loved the Harryhausen films so much - because I could finally see the dinosaurs move. I thought that was the coolest thing." After McCreery graduated from high school, music temporarily replaced his passion for art. Having learned to play the guitar, he joined a band that enabled him to earn a little money while touring cities throughout California. "My parents had always been very supportive of anything I did; so when I said I wanted to play the guitar, they let me do that, without any pressure. Of course, I got a lot of pressure from high school and college teachers who would say things like, 'You've got this talent for drawing - you've got to go out there and use it' I just didn't want to do that at the time, though. Art wasn't very challenging for me; so it wasn't very fulfilling, either." With the support of his parents, McCreery was able to live the footloose life of a traveling, sometime musician for nearly six years. Stan Winston Studio's next important project - James Cameron's Terminator 2 - had McCreery designing two permutations of the T-1000. Splash Head' would reveal the liquid metal character's head after being shot at close range, while 'Pretzel Man,' a similar effect, would provide a view of the entire body being blown apart. "Jim Cameron had very clear ideas in his own mind for Splash Head and Pretzel Man," McCreery noted, "but he wanted to see them on paper. I drew one version of Pretzel Man; but when I showed it to him, he said: 'No, no - that's not it at all. It's like this.' He drew this little stick figure on a napkin - and it was brilliant! The guy's a phenomenal artist. Every design he's ever done has blown me away." Rather than feel intimidated by the director's artistic talents, McCreery was - and continues to be - motivated by them. "I like working for people like Jim Cameron and Tim Burton and Steven Spielberg, even though there is a kind of pressure about it. There's no bullshitting with those guys, because every one of them could illustrate their ideas better than I could, if they had the time. They set some pretty high standards; but I love that. I work my best and my hardest when I'm scared." After Terminator 2, McCreery worked again with Tim Burton, designing the Penguin makeup Danny DeVito would wear in Batman Returns. "Tim came in with a little sketch of what he wanted the essence of the Penguin to be. It looked like something out of an Edward Gorey cartoon - which I thought was great because it was nothing like the Penguin look they'd had for Burgess Meredith in the Batman television series." The challenge came in recreating the look and style of Burton's sketch in the makeup, while retaining enough of DeVito's An early Crash McCreery concept - later extensively revised - for Kothoga in The Relic. features to ensure the actor would be recognizable. "We had to take all of these weird, quirky things about the design and somehow make it all come out looking like Danny DeVito. Fortunately, Danny was a real pleasure to work with. He came over for a makeup test; and as soon as he was in the makeup, he got into the character. To me, that is one of the most satisfying things about working at this studio - designing a character, and then getting to see it on the actor, knowing that your work is helping them to create a performance." With Steven Spielberg's Jurassic Park, the following year, McCreery was finally doing dinosaurs - and doing them in an entirely unprecedented fashion. "What was so exciting about being a part of Jurassic Park was that it was a whole new vision of dinosaurs, a whole new take on a kind of movie that had been done a million times before. This dinosaur movie was breaking the mold. We were dealing with new science and new ideas about what dinosaurs really were. For the first time, a film was going to show dinosaurs that were very active and warm-blooded and even intelligent." After years of drawing and admiring 'old-style' dinosaurs, however, McCreery did not immediately warm to this new take on the extinct animals. "At first I was saying, 'Oh, no - I like the dinosaurs in King Kong!' That's what dinosaurs were to me. It took me a while to realize that these new dinosaurs could be very exciting. They were more like animals you could relate to, that once lived on this earth. They weren't just monsters, or stupid lumbering beasts." Because the project was cloaked in secrecy in its early stages, McCreery worked in solitude on his dinosaur illustrations for Jurassic Park. "Stan put me up in this little room. I had my dinosaur books out and my music going - and I just drew dinosaurs all day long, every day for a year. It doesn't get any better than that." Once the film moved into actual production, Mccreery was released from the drawing board to serve as one of the on-set dinosaur puppeteers, wrangling radio- and cable-controlled performances from the prehistoric characters. After Jurassic Park, McCreery's talents went into helping to design makeups for Interview With the Vampire. Casting controversies and indecision regarding the role of Lestat translated into a series of false starts and delays for the conceptual team at Stan Winston Studio. McCreery devised a variety of makeups for Daniel Day Lewis, a one-time frontrunner for the role, and another for Jeremy Irons before Tom Cruise was finally cast. "It was a difficult situation for us,"remarked McCreery, "because in designing any makeup, we have to take into account the actor's physical characteristics. The movie's monster - a character with equal amounts of human, reptile and insect DNA comprising its genetic makeup - was problematic from the start, simply because it was the kind of creature that had already been seen in films such as the Alien trilogy and Predator. "A lot of films have characters that, physically, don't match up with their performances. A character will do something, and you'll think to yourself, 'That animal doesn't look like it could have done that.' For The Relic, I exaggerated the power of the beast, but kept it very animal-like so that it would fit into the setting of the museum." In one sense, McCreery could relate to the characters in The Relic, caught in a museum after hours, with lifelike animal exhibits that seem to breathe and watch, and maybe even move. Many of his days and nights are spent in Stan Winston's little shop of horrors, a place where predators and terminators and gray gorillas and raptors and vampires are on prominent display. The exhibits illustrate the singular talents of Stan Winston himself, and those of his artistic ensemble, But for Crash McCreery, they represent also the fulfillment of a childhood fantasy. "A real 747 goes through compression and decompression cycles," observed Boss visual effects supervisor David M. Jones, "so the skin takes on a characteristic wrinkle. It retains its original shape at the bulkheads and wherever it is riveted, but it tends to bow out at other places. We knew the Turbulence plane would be one of the older fuselages around; so we did some tests and added a kind of ripple to the surface of the fuselage, wings, tail and stabilizers. That gave us interesting reflections and shadows and light kicks off the plane - so it didn't have the kind of perfectly smooth surface that typically makes a miniature look like a toy." Slated to be filmed motion control, the model - which, at tenth-scale, weighed in the neighborhood of fourteen hundred pounds and was approximately the size of a small Cessna - was too large to be mounted from the tail on a standard model mover pipe rig. "If we'd tried to tail-mount this big model," remarked Jones, "twenty feet of it would have been cantilevered out in front. We were afraid that doing drastic plane movements with that kind of a setup would result in a lot of bounce, and we would not be able to get the motion control system to repeat precisely." To solve the problem, a special motion control rig was constructed by machine shop supervisor Bobby Johnston and lead motion control operator Duane McClintock. The rig resembled a giant marionette setup, with pairs of cables attached near the front of the model's fuselage section and on each wing, and connected to six motion control motors mounted above the plane. Not only did the rig provide a more stable mounting for the large model, it enabled the motion control photography crew to spin the plane on mutliple axes. The model's size was also a consideration in determining how it would be photographed. Whereas a blue- or greenscreen setup would be the standard method for executing the model photography, the large scale of the model jet - and relatively small Four large gimbals - including one capable of rotating a seventy-foot section of the full-size 747 set - were constructed by special effects coordinator Al Di Sarro and crew. scale of the shooting stage at Boss - called for a less common approach. "We were working in a fairly confined space," said Jones, "so the screen had to be positioned close to the model - which meant we would either get blue or green spill light on the miniature, or we'd have to take the extra time to flag the lights off of the model to shoot our matte passes." To avoid such complications, the decision was made to photograph the airplane in front of a screen coated with a fluorescent tangerine-colored paint, illuminated by ultraviolet light. "By using the black light, we got a nice saturated color on the screen; and, assuming the model wasn't painted with something that would fluoresce, we wouldn't have to worry about getting spill light on it. Even if we did get light spill on the plane, it would be royal blue - easy to remove since it was so different from the tangerine." New motion control software, written by Bill Thomas of Kuper Controls, was employed to transfer plane movements - choreographed in a series of animatics - to the motion control system. "In theory," explained Jones, "we could build the whole stage and camera setup in the computer, then take the roll, axis, tilt and all of those numbers from the animatic and read them into the motion control unit. However, that theory did not really apply in practice. Although we were able to use those numbers directly from time to time, they didn't track exactly because we didn't have time to make virtual lenses that perfectly matched the lenses we were using on stage. So we'd take a general position of the plane from the animatic and put that into the system, then go to another key frame in the animatic and match that position. It wound up being kind of a half-and-half procedure, but it still sped things up. On average, we shot and programmed a move every two and a half days - which is fast for really tight motion control photography." Aerial backgrounds for the miniature 747 were simulated through practical means at Boss Film. "Distant background clouds were made by stuffing cotton into chicken wire," said production visual effects producer Brian Frankish, "and those were positioned several feet in front of a neutral gray cyclorama. Within the clouds themselves, a variety CINEFEX 69 • 135

of flash bulbs were used to create a series of practical light flashes." While the practical approach sufficed for distant backgrounds, more prominent and interactive cloud formations were achieved digitally. "An attempt had been made to create midground and foreground clouds with smoke elements," stated Boss digital effects supervisor Tom Dadras, "but there was no way to adequately control the smoke. At that point, we decided to try a digital approach, creating multiplane clouds that moved quickly past camera and dissipated as the plane traveled through them. It was something that hadn't been done to this extent before, so we had to prove to our own effects supervisors and the clients that we could pull it off. To create a completely realistic look, we had to simulate a thick layering of clouds with appropriate variations in density, patchiness and movement. On top of that, we had to make it look like a storm environment." After some experimentation, Dadras and his team hit upon the most satisfactory technique for realizing the digital clouds: CG artists would paint 2-D cloud planes and move them in 3-D space. "For some shots we had as many as thirty or forty layers "and it was those of 2-D clouds," remarked Dadras, multiple layers, and the way they interacted, that created a sense of three-dimensional clouds. We scaled and translated the 2-D clouds as needed for each scene - so in one scene it would look as if they were flying away from us, while in another it would look as if they were coming straight at camera." The most delicate and exacting of the shots were those featuring the plane moving through cloud formations, requiring simulated interaction between the model photography and the digitally produced atmosphere. "Looking at reference footage of planes moving through clouds, we found that the clouds don't really break up as a result - specific areas just fade out a bit as the plane makes contact, and then fade back up as it passes through. To simulate that, we placed cloud layers both behind and in front of the plane, fading one out as we faded up the other. So it was a matter of crossdissolving layers in sequence to make it look as if the plane was moving through them." Just as they had done for the live-action cloud footage, Pacific Title Digital tweaked some of the Boss aerial backgrounds, color correcting them to simulate darker, stormier skies. The practical 747 model was replaced with a CG version for specific distant views of the plane, or for shots in which the airplane was required to 136 * CINEFEX 69 make a particularly dynamic move. One such shot revealed the storm-tossed jet doing a 180-degree rollover. "To completely rotate a twenty-three-foot model on stage would have been a massive rigging problem," Vargo noted, "so we decided to have Boss create a CG plane to do the rollover. This approach probably saved us a week and a half on the stage - which more than paid for the cost of the CG planei To build the 747 computer model, a digitizing arm was employed to scan the miniature. Animation was implemented in Wavefront, while RenderMan was utilized to create the final image. "The task required absolute accuracy in textures and lighting," said Tom Dadras. "We had to match both the real plane and the miniature, all the way down to the tail logo light." In a hair-raising finale, the aircraft - piloted by Halloran - suffers a series of near-disastrous collisions on its approach into Los Angeles International Airport. For closeups of the plane's landing gear grazing various buildings, special effects coordinator Al Di Sarro and his crew built a large gantry rig to support an authentic 9000-pound, four-wheel landing gear assembly from a Boeing 707 - the differences between the 707 gear and that on a 747 having been judged insignificant. The gantry consisted of an overhead track system, chain-driven by a 350-horsepower Chevy engine. Set up inside a warehouse, the gantry rig enabled the physical effects crew to move the massive assemblage at thirty-five to forty miles per hour. The nose gear from a 747 was also mounted on the gantry rig and filmed for a scene in which the descending plane slams into a rooftop karaoke bar. The initial shot, as seen from the approaching airliner, was accomplished by compositing a computer generated bar atop live-action footage of the Crown Plaza Hotel in Los Angeles. For subsequent views of the plane moving through the rooftop bar, a false front was erected inside the warehouse, then decimated by the moving gantry rig and nose gear. In postproduction, photography of the model 747 was composited and tracked to the practical nose gear footage by Boss Film. The shot was so effective, Vargo decided to use the rig for a scene in which the airplane skids over a parking garage. "We built a new set around the gantry," said Vargo, "mocking up a parking garage beneath it. The set consisted of a retaining wall and painted parking lanes, with translights hung all around. We dressed it with a lot of stripped-down cars, which were easily pushed aside by the massive rig." The gantry was also used for a shot of a Ford pickup being ensnared by the landing gear, as well as later shots of the plane attempting a landing at LAX with the attached pickup scraping along the runway. "It took about six months to build the gantry rig, and it was the hardest thing to shoot - but it gave us a lot of bang for the buck. It's what people remember and talk about when they see the movie." Al Di Sarro's team also built four large gimbals, designed by Bob Graham and constructed by Jim Guarrera and crew, for several of the film's dramatic interior sequences. The largest of the four - bigger than any built previously for film production - was a thirty-five-foot-tall gimbal, made of 150 tons of steel. Capable of holding a seventy-foot section of the plane and turning it 360 degrees in just eleven seconds, it was used for some of the interior shots in the plane rollover sequence, as well as several of the more violent shakeups. The longest gimbal was able to lift a 170-foot section of the plane up to three feet in the air, then rock and shake it to simulate severe turbulence. Two additional speed gimbals were designed to rotate smaller sections of the plane up to 45 degrees in less than five seconds, and could also be used to simulate a steep dive or extreme ascent. Included in the plane-approach sequence was a scene of cars being pushed over the edge of the parking structure, supposedly by the descending plane. The gag had been photographed at an actual garage, but the resulting footage lacked dramatic impact. "In the garage footage, there was one lowangle view of the cars falling over the edge," Vargo remarked, "but the plane wasn't visible in the shot. We could have added it with model photography, but that would have been expensive. So I suggested that we go out to the airport and shoot a real plane. I talked to the people at LAX, got the arrival schedules for all the incoming 747s and found out which runways they would be using. Then we set up our cameras and filmed all the silver-bottomed 747s as they came iniVargo determined which of the incoming plane shots was the most suitable, then turned it over to John La Fauce at Pacific Title Digital, where it was composited into the live-action parking garage footage. Reflecting on the scenes of aerial mayhem that have audiences gripping their armrests, Mark Vargo is more than pleased with the visual effects work in Turbulence. "I think we put some images on the screen that have raised the bar - certainly in terms of aerial work. And in the process, I also learned a tremendous amount about digital technology"

The Henson team built approximately fifty animatronic puppies for the show, using a wide variety of materials and techniques. "As always," related Scanlan, "we weren't trying to duplicate nature, but cut to the essence of what nature is. We asked ourselves, 'What do people actually see and notice when they look at a puppy?' And we realized that one of the elements people instantly recognize and remember is a puppy's baggy skin. So we were very keen on creating loose, baggy skins for the puppies." Those skins were produced in various combinations of silicones, urethane and foam latex, depending on the character and its actions in the film. "By building the character from the inside out, we were able to allow the skin to remain free to move, a technique we learned from Babe. In areas that were not covered in hair - such as the nose, eyelids and the edges of the mouth - silicone pieces were employed." Puppy fur was affixed through flocking, which worked especially well for the short-haired Dalmatians. Various black-and-white patterns - already established in the live dogs - were then applied. "The size and body form varied from one puppy to another and from one batch of puppies to the next," Scanlan stated. "Some would have longer noses or would be more narrow in the face. But we found that people picked up on the patterns of blackand-white and on the spots more than anything else - and that worked in our favor. As long as the pattern was consistent for each puppy character, no one seemed to notice if Fidget had a longer nose in one scene than he had in another. So for each scene, we would come in with a fairly bland pattern on the puppy; then we would airbrush it to make it look more like the puppy we were supposed to be matching for that scene." "The remote puppies were like little self-contained robots," Scanian related, "operated remotely by our computer-driven performance system. The cablecontrolled puppets allowed us to get a higher level of performance and mobility than the remote units; but because of the rods and cables, they were only used for scenes where a puppy might appear from behind an object or a piece of furniture. The hand puppets were used for shots involving the puppies' heads only, such as through a hole in the chair." The ten puppy characters with the most prominent roles were built in all three mechanical configurations, while specialty puppies were also fabricated for specific scenes or actions. "For instance, Fidget continually scratches his ear - so we tashioned a Fidget puppy just for scratching." Another puppy requiring special mechanization was Wizzer - so named because of his propensity for urinating at inopportune times and places. "Wizzer was fitted with a tube that ran from the head to the tail area. We would feed liquid in at the head and pump it through on cue." Sleeping puppies were equipped with simple breathing mechanisms and were rodpuppeteered from below. Ten newborn puppies were also built. Based on six-day-old pups, the newborns were fashioned in silicone gel to make them soft and pliable. "Those ten puppies were actually put in with a real litter of newborns, shot at a breeder's home, immediately after the puppies had been born," recalled Scanlan. Utilizing motion capture information, a fixed pivot mechanism was constructed, actuated by levers. By pulling those levers in a certain sequence, we could get the horse body to rear up, the legs to retract and then push outwards and kick the barn door. This scene was closely choreographed in conjunction with the stunt supervisor. It was a sequential thing, powered by large cables that ran out of the horse's neck. The body was able to pivot from the front legs to get that initial lift into the air, and then the actual kick was done using cables." Three raccoons that foil Cruella's henchmen were represented by Henson rod puppets in some shots, while other scenes employed live animals. "The raccoons had animatronic heads and mechanized hands and feet," Scanlan explained, "but the 142 * CINEFEX 69 gross movements of the body and the arms were achieved with rods. In nearly all situations, we were able to do rod-actuated shots without resorting to rod removal, just by framing or hiding things carefully." The hair of the raccoons was hand-punched, rather than flocked, to create a realistic and natural look. "One of our problems these days is that we are using so much artificial fur - mainly because we now live in a political climate that frowns on the use of real fur. But artificial fur doesn't have quite the same look, no matter how good it is. So, in the case of the raccoons, we had to do some very skillful blending to make it look as real as possible." For the character of Kipper, the Airedale that helps the puppies to escape Cruella's clutches, the Henson team built a full-body, rod-actuated puppet that could be quickly modified to serve as a hand "We could remove the lower puppet for closeups. section of the stomach," said Scanlan, "allowing a performer's arm to go up inside to hand-operate the neck. The head itself was animatronic, driven through the computer controlled performance system, but the armature also allowed us to connect rods to him for body movements." The entire slate of animatronics and hand puppets was built within a seven-month period. "It was tight," observed Scanlan, "but, fortunately, I had the same great team that had worked on Babe, as well as many of the UK's most experienced people. The two projects were so closely related that even though it was a very short schedule, our previous experience, careful planning and the assistance of ILM enabled us to build only what was really needed. That was a great bonus to us." In all of the public and critical response to 101 Dalmatians, little attention was given to the mechanical and digital effects that had made the movie possible - and that was as it should be. Employed sparingly and artfully, the two effects disciplines managed to avoid tripping over both the live-action elements and each other. "In this show," said Owens, "animatronics and CG went together in a perfect way, both artistically and technically. Neal Scanlan would often be the first to say, 'No, that would look better as a CG shot than it would as an animatronic.' Everyone was committed to finding the best effects technique for every shot. The thing is, you either have to spend the time on the set with animatronics, or you have to spend the time in postproduction for CG. But with all of the options available, someone will inevitably find new combinations of effects that will offer some very convincing solutions to filmmaking problems." THE SIXTH MAN (continued from page 56) greenscreen positioned behind the actor so that his image - which would not have the painting effect - could be matted into the scene. "The greenscreen was about a foot off the ground, so we had to go in and roto Kadeem's feet through the entire shot," explained Van Vliet. "But we were still able to extract a terrific matte off of it Fortunately we didn't have to put a texture on Kadeem. The software we used doesn't react kindly to radical movement, and it would have been flickering and chopping all over the place. When it was all done, we took the finished composite and put a move on it to make it less static looking." Special lighting effects throughout the film, by director of photography Michael Ozier, would end up inadvertently complicating the visual effects task. "Mike came up with a really great technique in which he used a big blue xenon key light to follow the ghost around," Van Vliet elaborated. "The effect looked great; but later, in postproduction, we had a difficult time trying to achieve that same burned-in look for the rim light on our CG models. In the computer environment, that light is painted in instead of being burned into film - so there's a big difference in perceived luminance. Also, the intensity of the xenon light created a halation effect around the ghost: and whenever we did fullbody rotoing we would lose that overexposed glow and it would start to look cut out. Eventually we got it working pretty well, but not without a huge amount of digital massage." Despite his heavy reliance on digital technology for The Sixth Man, John Van Vliet is nevertheless determined to hang onto his optical options. "The computer was really great at being able to do minute adjustments. We could tweak to an nth degree. But the realities of any production are that sometimes you just have to go very hard and very fast. Our optical printer helped us communicate with the director - we were able to make enormous jumps in the information path by just going downstairs and doing a quick test and slapping together a double exposure. So even with a show like this, where the final output was almost entirely digital, optical techniques played a very important background role. In my book, their position in the food chain is still assured."
